heading: How Riak TS Processes SQL Queries#
text: Assume we have way too many computers and we aren’t sure why one of them is being unreliable. We think it’s running hot but we’re not sure, so we’re going to look at our metrics data and see whether or not it is. In particular, we want to ask about the last forty minutes of CPU temperature data for bunnahabhain.islay with temperatures over 50°C.

title: SQL for Riak TS
heading: How Riak TS Processes SQL Queries#
text: We think it’s running hot but we’re not sure, so we’re going to look at our metrics data and see whether or not it is. In particular, we want to ask about the last forty minutes of CPU temperature data for bunnahabhain.islay with temperatures over 50°C. Our SQL query looks like:

title: SQL for Riak TS
heading: How Riak TS Processes SQL Queries#
text: In particular, we want to ask about the last forty minutes of CPU temperature data for bunnahabhain.islay with temperatures over 50°C. Our SQL query looks like: SQL

title: SQL for Riak TS
heading: How Riak TS Processes SQL Queries#
text: SQL SELECT * FROM metrics WHERE hostname='bunnahabhain.islay' AND metric_name='core_temp' AND time < 1446762821844 AND time > 1446760421844 AND metric_value > 50.0;

title: SQL for Riak TS
heading: How Riak TS Processes SQL Queries#
text: And we send the query to Riak TS. Once the query is sent to Riak TS the following happens:

title: SQL for Riak TS
heading: How Riak TS Processes SQL Queries#
text: Once the query is sent to Riak TS the following happens: The planner receives the query from you and parses it. The parser isolates the table name, and then the parser constructs a tree out of the `WHERE` conditions, and identifies `WHERE` predicates that are connected with `AND` operations. The planner then loads the table’s DDL. Then the planner plucks out the `WHERE` conditions that are fields in the DDL’s primary key. And then the planner uses the `WHERE` conditions and the DDL’s partition key (a quantized primary key) to calculate coverage; in this case, the three partitions that contain rows matching the query. Finally, the planner creates a filter based on the `metric_value` `WHERE` condition and sends it to the three partitions. Each partition loops over its data, matching rows against the filter. The partitions then send their matched rows back to the planner. The planner then collects the matched rows and returns them to you.

title: Architecture of Riak TS Tables
heading: Riak TS Tables#
text: With Riak TS, you no longer have to build your own time series database on Riak KV. Instead, Riak TS integrates SQL structure and functionality with Riak KV key/value storage. It does this through Riak TS tables that you customize to fit your time series data and the needs of your workflow.

heading: Data Modeling#
text: The column names in the partition key are used to determine which vnodes handle the writes and queries, which is why we suggest using a column definition that captures a class or type of data and another that captures an instance of that class or type. For instance, `region` represents a class of data, whereas `state` is an instance of that class. If both column names represent the same class or type of data for large numbers of writes, and the quanta that is specified has a large duration, only n_val vnodes will process the incoming writes.

title: Timestamps
text: Timestamps in Riak TS are a critical data type, nearly always a part of partition key. They are often leveraged with the quantum function to group data by 15 minute clumps, or 10 second clumps, or 60 day clumps, et cetera, depending on how quickly your time series data come in and how you need to analyze them.

title: Timestamps
heading: Unix Epoch Time#
text: Timestamps in Riak TS are stored as positive integers representing the number of UTC milliseconds since January 1st, 1970 (UNIX epoch time). As an example: midnight GMT, August 1st 2016, would exist in the database as the integer `1470009600000`. You can read more about UNIX epoch time here.

title: Timestamps
heading: ISO 8601#
text: For INSERT and SELECT statements, Riak TS supports ISO 8601 strings which are converted to UTC milliseconds. A Note on ISO 8601 Support ISO 8601 support is useful for casual interactions via riak shell, but we do NOT recommend using ISO 8601 in production applications. Instead, use the TS-supported client libraries to pass timestamps as integers for better performance and correctness.

title: Timestamps
heading: Reduced Accuracy#
text: Strings that do not include seconds are referred to as reduced accuracy representations. Ambiguity can arise with reduced accuracy representations. For instance, what do the comparisons `time > '2015'` or `time <= '2003-05-01T05:10'` mean when translated to epoch time value as stored in Riak TS?

title: Timestamps
heading: Reduced Accuracy#

To resolve those ambiguities, Riak TS expands the reduced accuracy value to the lowest date/time which matches the specification. `2015` becomes `2015-01-01 00:00:00`. `2003-05-01T05:10` becomes `2003-05-01T05:10:00`.

heading: Time Zone FAQs#
text: Why can’t Riak TS default to the operating system’s time zone instead of GMT if `riak-admin` is not used to set a time zone? It is critically important that all servers in the cluster agree on the time zone to be used for translating time strings into timestamps. Defaulting to the operating system’s time zone is only safe if all servers in the cluster are guaranteed to be configured identically.

title: Timestamps
heading: Unsupported Formats#
text: ISO 8601 includes three notable syntaxes which are not yet supported in Riak TS: expanded representation (years outside the range 0000-9999), time intervals (a range of times), and week dates (a week or day expressed as a number of weeks into the year).

title: Riak TS Release Notes
text: Released August 24, 2016. Riak TS 1.4.0 delivers a broad range of new functionality and improvements, including:

title: Riak TS Release Notes
text: Riak TS 1.4.0 delivers a broad range of new functionality and improvements, including: GROUP BY, a SQL statement used with `SELECT` Simplified time/date parsing and ISO 8601 support Rolling Upgrade/Downgrade support Global data expiry (per cluster) New SHOW TABLES SQL statement Enhanced `DESCRIBE`

title: Riak TS Release Notes
heading: New Features#
text: The GROUP BY statement allows you to pick out and condense rows sharing the same value into a single row. You can read more about `GROUP BY` here. [PR #1445] [riak_core PR #848] [riak_ql PR #132] [PR #1445] [riak_core PR #848] [riak_ql PR #132] ISO 8601 strings are now supported as timestamps for SELECT and INSERT statements in Riak TS. You can find out more about timestamps and ISO 8601 here. [PR #1444] [riak_core PR #847] [riak PR #862] [riak_ee PR #403] [riak_shell PR #43] [PR #1444] [riak_core PR #847] [riak PR #862] [riak_ee PR #403] [riak_shell PR #43]

title: Riak TS Release Notes
heading: New Features#
text: You can now configure global object expiry (a.k.a. time to live - TTL) for your Riak TS data. Read more about data expiry here. [eleveldb PR #210] [eleveldb PR #210] `SHOW TABLES`, which lists all the TS tables you’ve created, is now available. You can read more about the SHOW TABLES statement here. [riak_ql PR #133] [PR #1448] [riak_shell PR #44] [riak_ql PR #133] [PR #1448] [riak_shell PR #44] Riak TS 1.4.0 supports rolling upgrades from 1.3.1 and downgrades to 1.3.1. You can read about how to perform an upgrade or downgrade here.

title: Riak TS Release Notes
heading: New Features#
text: Note on Downgrading If you freshly installed TS 1.4.0 and did NOT upgrade from 1.3.1, and then you choose to downgrade to 1.3.1, you will need to change your riak.conf to preserve your configuration settings. Read more about that process here.

title: Riak TS Release Notes
heading: Additions#
text: New configuration settings for Riak TS have been added to riak.conf. You can read more about TS’s configuration options here. Additionally, the old configuration settings have been exposed and are being deprecated. If you were using the old configuration settings, please update riak.conf to use the new settings. The older settings are scheduled to be deprecated.

title: Riak TS Release Notes
heading: Changes#
text: Riak TS now has some TS-specific security settings. You can read more about security topics in Riak TS here. [PR #1452] The DESCRIBE statement now returns additional information about the interval and unit of time in your TS table. [PR #1438] LevelDB now uses LZ4 as an internal compression mechanism. This change should provide a performance boost for LevelDB. [PR #208]

title: Riak TS Release Notes
heading: Bugfixes#
text: [PR #1428] The security permissions for Riak TS’s protocol buffer API have been fixed to return in the correct format of a string rather than an atom. [riak_ql PR#126] `INSERT` now accepts booleans as a valid data type. [repl PR#744] When using Riak TS Enterprise, do not push time series data to the realtime replication queue unless it is enabled. [riak_ql #130] Only one table at a time may be queried with `SELECT` and now there is a better error message if you try to query more than one table. [riak_shell #39] Fix some typos in riak shell’s help text. [PR #1439] When building a query an error could result if a string was used. This has been fixed.

title: Riak TS Release Notes
heading: Compatibility#
text: Riak TS is compatible with the following:

title: Riak TS Release Notes
heading: Compatibility#
text: Riak TS is compatible with the following: RHEL/CentOS 6 RHEL/CentOS 7 Ubuntu 12.04 LTS Ubuntu 14.04 LTS Debian 7 (development only) Debian 8 (development only) OS X 10.8+ (development only) AWS Marketplace

title: Riak TS Release Notes
heading: Known Issues#
text: The list_keys API may be unreliable in clusters containing a mix of TS 1.3.1 and TS 1.4 nodes. AAE must be turned off. Riak Search, and subsequently Solr, is not supported for TS. HTTP API security is not supported. Security checks are included in the code path, but the permissions are not registered with riak_core, so enabling security in HTTP means disabling any TS functionality. See the code here. Bitcask backend must not be used with Riak TS.

title: Downgrading Riak TS
text: Downgrades of Riak TS are tested and supported for two feature release versions, with the general procedure similar to a rolling upgrade.

title: Downgrading Riak TS
heading: Debian/Ubuntu#
text: The following example demonstrates downgrading a Riak TS node that has been installed with the Debian/Ubuntu packages provided by Basho. You should perform the following actions on each node: 1.

heading: Debian/Ubuntu#

heading: Debian/Ubuntu#

title: Downgrading Riak TS
heading: Debian/Ubuntu#

title: Downgrading Riak TS

title: Downgrading Riak TS
heading: Debian/Ubuntu#

heading: Debian/Ubuntu#

title: Downgrading Riak TS

title: Downgrading Riak TS
heading: Debian/Ubuntu#

title: Downgrading Riak TS
heading: Debian/Ubuntu#

title: Downgrading Riak TS

title: Downgrading Riak TS

title: Installing on AWS Marketplace
text: Riak TS can be installed on AWS virtual machines (VMs) using a binary package available here. This page will walk you through the process of setting up your AWS environment and installing Riak TS on it.

title: Installing on AWS Marketplace
heading: Launch Riak VMs via the AWS Marketplace#
text: Get started by launching a Riak TS virtual machine via the AWS Marketplace. (You will need an Amazon Web Services account.)

title: Installing on AWS Marketplace
heading: Launch Riak VMs via the AWS Marketplace#
text: (You will need an Amazon Web Services account.) Navigate to https://aws.amazon.com/marketplace/ and sign in with your Amazon Web Services account. Locate Riak TS in the Databases & Caching category or search for Riak TS from any page. Set your desired AWS region, EC2 instance type, firewall settings, and key pair. Then click the Accept Terms and Launch with 1-Click button.

title: Installing on AWS Marketplace
heading: Security Group Settings#
text: Once the virtual machine is created, you should verify that your selected EC2 security group is properly configured for Riak TS.

text: Once the virtual machine is created, you should verify that your selected EC2 security group is properly configured for Riak TS. In the AWS EC2 Management Console, click Security Groups, then click the name of the security group for your Riak TS VM. Click on the Inbound tab in the lower pane. Your security group should include the following open ports:

title: Installing on AWS Marketplace

text: You will need need to launch at least 3 instances to form a Riak cluster. When the instances have been provisioned and the security group is configured, you can connect to them using SSH or PuTTY as the ec2-user. You can find more information on connecting to an instance on the official Amazon EC2 instance guide.

heading: Create a Riak Cluster on AWS#
text: When the instances have been provisioned and the security group is configured, you can connect to them using SSH or PuTTY as the ec2-user. You can find more information on connecting to an instance on the official Amazon EC2 instance guide. Note The following clustering setup will not be resilient to instance restarts unless deployed in Amazon VPC.

title: Installing on AWS Marketplace
heading: Create a Riak Cluster on AWS#
text: Note The following clustering setup will not be resilient to instance restarts unless deployed in Amazon VPC. On the first node, obtain the internal IP address: Bash curl http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/local-ipv4 For all other nodes, use the internal IP address of the first node: Bash sudo riak-admin cluster join riak@<ip.of.first.node> After all of the nodes are joined, execute the following: Bash sudo riak-admin cluster plan If this looks good: Bash sudo riak-admin cluster commit To check the status of clustering use: Bash sudo riak-admin member_status

title: Installing on AWS Marketplace
heading: Create a Riak Cluster on AWS#
text: You now have a Riak cluster running on AWS.

title: Installing on AWS Marketplace
heading: Configure riak shell#
text: In order to function, riak shell must know about each node in the cluster.

title: Installing on AWS Marketplace
heading: Configure riak shell#
text: In order to function, riak shell must know about each node in the cluster. On each node, obtain the internal IP addresses: Bash curl http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/local-ipv4 On each node in the cluster, edit `/etc/riak/riak_shell.config`, adding the IPs of each node. You should end up with a config that is similar to: Text %%% -*- erlang -*- [ {riak_shell, [ {logging, off}, {cookie, riak}, {show_connection_status, false}, {nodes, [ riak@10.13.37.221, riak@10.22.19.97, riak@10.2.54.31 ]} ]} ].

title: Installing on AWS Marketplace
heading: Configure riak shell#
text: Run `riak-shell` and ping the nodes to test the configuration: Bash sudo riak-shell You should see a riak shell prompt: Bash [ec2-user ~]$ sudo riak-shell Erlang R16B02_basho10 (erts-5.10.3) [source] [64-bit] [smp:2:2] [async-threads:10] [hipe] [kernel-poll:false] [frame-pointer] version "riak_shell 0.9/sql 1.3", use 'quit;' or 'q;' to exit or 'help;' for helpConnected... riak-shell(1)> Run a `ping` to test the configuration: Bash riak-shell(1)>ping; 'riak@10.13.37.221': (connected) 'riak@10.22.19.97': (connected) 'riak@10.2.54.31': (connected) riak-shell(2)>

title: Installing on Mac OS X
text: Riak TS can be installed on Mac OS X systems using a binary package available here. Note Mac OS X is only supported for developing with Riak TS and NOT for general operations.

title: Installing on Mac OS X
heading: `ulimit`#
text: OS X gives you a very small limit on open file handles. Even with a backend that uses very few file handles, it’s possible to run out. See Open Files Limit for more information about changing the limit.

title: Installing on Mac OS X
heading: Install Riak TS#
text: To install Riak TS on your Mac, download the package and then run: Bash

title: Installing on Mac OS X
heading: Install Riak TS#
text: Bash tar zxvf riak-ts-1.4.0-OSX-x86_64.tar.gz cd riak-ts-1.4.0

title: Installing on Mac OS X
heading: Start your Riak TS node#

title: Installing on Mac OS X
heading: Start your Riak TS node#

heading: Verify Riak TS is running#

title: Installing on Mac OS X

title: Upgrading Riak TS
text: Note on upgrading Riak TS from older versions Upgrading Riak TS is only supported for Riak TS 1.3.1 to 1.4.0. For assistance upgrading from earlier versions to 1.4.0 contact Client Services. If you run Riak Control, you should disable it during the rolling upgrade process.

title: Upgrading Riak TS
text: For assistance upgrading from earlier versions to 1.4.0 contact Client Services. If you run Riak Control, you should disable it during the rolling upgrade process. Riak TS nodes negotiate with each other to determine supported operating modes.

title: Upgrading Riak TS
text: If you run Riak Control, you should disable it during the rolling upgrade process. Riak TS nodes negotiate with each other to determine supported operating modes. This allows clusters containing mixed-versions of Riak TS to properly interoperate without special configuration, and simplifies rolling upgrades.

title: Upgrading Riak TS
heading: Debian/Ubuntu#
text: The following example demonstrates upgrading a Riak TS node that has been installed with the Debian/Ubuntu packages provided by Basho. 1. Stop Riak TS:

title: Upgrading Riak TS
heading: Debian/Ubuntu#
text: 1. Stop Riak TS: Bash

title: Upgrading Riak TS
heading: Debian/Ubuntu#
text: Bash riak stop

title: Upgrading Riak TS
heading: Debian/Ubuntu#
text: 2. Back up the Riak TS node’s `/etc` and `/data` directories: Bash

title: Upgrading Riak TS
heading: Debian/Ubuntu#
text: Bash sudo tar -czf riak_backup.tar.gz /var/lib/riak /etc/riak

title: Upgrading Riak TS
heading: Debian/Ubuntu#
text: 3. Upgrade Riak TS: Bash

title: Upgrading Riak TS
heading: Debian/Ubuntu#
text: Bash sudo dpkg -i »riakts_package_name«.deb

title: Upgrading Riak TS
heading: Debian/Ubuntu#
text: 4. Restart Riak TS: Note Before restarting Riak TS, check your ‘riak.conf’ file and verify that your settings are configured as expected.

title: Upgrading Riak TS
heading: Debian/Ubuntu#
text: Restart Riak TS: Note Before restarting Riak TS, check your ‘riak.conf’ file and verify that your settings are configured as expected. Bash

title: Upgrading Riak TS
heading: Debian/Ubuntu#
text: Bash riak start

title: Upgrading Riak TS
heading: Debian/Ubuntu#
text: 5. Verify Riak TS is running the new version: Bash

title: Upgrading Riak TS
heading: Debian/Ubuntu#
text: Bash riak version

title: Upgrading Riak TS
heading: Debian/Ubuntu#
text: 6. Wait for the `riak_kv` service to start: Bash

title: Upgrading Riak TS
heading: Debian/Ubuntu#
text: Bash riak-admin wait-for-service riak_kv »target node«

title: Upgrading Riak TS
heading: Debian/Ubuntu#
text: `»target node«` is the node which you have just upgraded (e.g. `riak@192.168.1.11`)

title: Upgrading Riak TS
heading: Debian/Ubuntu#
text: 7. Wait for any hinted handoff transfers to complete: Bash

title: Upgrading Riak TS
heading: Debian/Ubuntu#
text: Bash riak-admin transfers

title: Upgrading Riak TS
heading: Debian/Ubuntu#
text: While the node was offline, other nodes may have accepted writes on its behalf. This data is transferred to the node when it becomes available.

title: Upgrading Riak TS
heading: Debian/Ubuntu#
text: 8. Repeat the process for the remaining nodes in the cluster.

title: Upgrading Riak TS
heading: RHEL/CentOS#
text: The following example demonstrates upgrading a Riak TS node that has been installed with the RHEL/CentOS packages provided by Basho. 1. Stop Riak TS:

title: Upgrading Riak TS
heading: RHEL/CentOS#
text: 1. Stop Riak TS: Bash

title: Upgrading Riak TS
heading: RHEL/CentOS#
text: Bash riak stop

title: Upgrading Riak TS
heading: RHEL/CentOS#
text: 2. Back up Riak TS’s `/etc` and `/data` directories: Bash

title: Upgrading Riak TS
heading: RHEL/CentOS#
text: Bash sudo tar -czf riak_backup.tar.gz /var/lib/riak /etc/riak

title: Upgrading Riak TS
heading: RHEL/CentOS#
text: 3. Upgrade Riak TS: Bash

title: Upgrading Riak TS
heading: RHEL/CentOS#
text: Bash sudo rpm -Uvh »riakts_package_name«.rpm

title: Upgrading Riak TS
heading: RHEL/CentOS#
text: 4. Restart Riak TS: Note Before restarting Riak TS, check your ‘riak.conf’ file and verify that your settings are configured as expected.

title: Upgrading Riak TS
heading: RHEL/CentOS#
text: Restart Riak TS: Note Before restarting Riak TS, check your ‘riak.conf’ file and verify that your settings are configured as expected. Bash

title: Upgrading Riak TS
heading: RHEL/CentOS#
text: Bash riak start

title: Upgrading Riak TS
heading: RHEL/CentOS#
text: 5. Verify that Riak TS is running the new version: Bash

title: Upgrading Riak TS
heading: RHEL/CentOS#
text: Bash riak version

title: Upgrading Riak TS
heading: RHEL/CentOS#
text: 6. Wait for the `riak_kv` service to start: Bash

title: Upgrading Riak TS
heading: RHEL/CentOS#
text: Bash riak-admin wait-for-service riak_kv »target node«

title: Upgrading Riak TS
heading: RHEL/CentOS#
text: `»target node«` is the node which you have just upgraded (e.g. riak@192.168.1.11)

title: Upgrading Riak TS
heading: RHEL/CentOS#
text: 7. Wait for any hinted handoff transfers to complete: Bash

title: Upgrading Riak TS
heading: RHEL/CentOS#
text: Bash riak-admin transfers

title: Upgrading Riak TS
heading: RHEL/CentOS#
text: While the node was offline, other nodes may have accepted writes on its behalf. This data is transferred to the node when it becomes available.

title: Upgrading Riak TS
heading: RHEL/CentOS#
text: 8. Repeat the process for the remaining nodes in the cluster.

title: Upgrading Riak TS
heading: Rolling Upgrade to Enterprise#
text: If you would like to upgrade an existing Riak TS cluster to a commercially supported Riak TS Enterprise cluster with multi-datacenter replication, undertake the following steps:

title: Upgrading Riak TS
heading: Rolling Upgrade to Enterprise#
text: If you would like to upgrade an existing Riak TS cluster to a commercially supported Riak TS Enterprise cluster with multi-datacenter replication, undertake the following steps: Back up your `/etc` (riak.conf and vm.args) and `/data` directories. Shut down the node you are going to upgrade. Uninstall your Riak TS package. Install the `riak-ts-ee` package. A standard package uninstall should not have removed your data directories. If it did, move your backup to where the data directory should be. Copy any customizations from your backed-up vm.args file to the `riak-ts-ee` installed vm.args file, these files may be identical.

title: Upgrading Riak TS
heading: Rolling Upgrade to Enterprise#
text: The riak.conf file from `riak-ts-ee` will be significantly different from your backed-up file. While it will contain all of the same sections as your original, it will have many new ones. Copy the customizations from your original riak.conf file into the appropriate sections in the new one. Ensure that the following sections are present in riak.conf:

title: Upgrading Riak TS
heading: Rolling Upgrade to Enterprise#
text: `riak_core` — the `cluster_mgr` setting must be present. See MDC v3 Configuration for more information. `riak_repl` — See MDC v3 Configuration for more information. `riak_jmx` — See JMX Monitoring for more information. `snmp` — See SNMP for more information.

title: Upgrading Riak TS
heading: Rolling Upgrade to Enterprise#
text: Start Riak TS on the upgraded node.

title: Upgrading Riak TS
heading: Basho Patches#
text: After upgrading, you should ensure that any custom patches contained in the `basho-patches` directory are examined to determine their application to the upgraded version. If you find that patches no longer apply to the upgraded version, you should remove them from the `basho-patches` directory prior to operating the node in production. The following lists locations of the `basho-patches` directory for each supported operating system:

title: Upgrading Riak TS
heading: Basho Patches#
text: The following lists locations of the `basho-patches` directory for each supported operating system: CentOS & RHEL Linux: `/usr/lib64/riak/lib/basho-patches` Debian & Ubuntu Linux: `/usr/lib/riak/lib/basho-patches`

title: Configure Riak TS
text: Riak TS exposes a few configuration settings in riak.conf. This document will walk you through the TS configurations. Deprecation Warning The Riak TS configuration settings in riak.conf have changed.

title: Configure Riak TS
text: This document will walk you through the TS configurations. Deprecation Warning The Riak TS configuration settings in riak.conf have changed. The old settings will be deprecated.

title: Configure Riak TS
text: Deprecation Warning The Riak TS configuration settings in riak.conf have changed. The old settings will be deprecated. Please update your riak.conf with the new settings.

title: Configure Riak TS
heading: Configuration options#
text: Make certain the configuration file on each node gets the same parameters to avoid inconsistent behavior. Benchmarking of your use cases and traffic load is recommended when changing these parameters. Settings which are too permissive can result in a slow database under heavy load.

title: Configure Riak TS
heading: Timeout#
text: Use `riak_kv.query.timeseries.timeout` to configure the timeout for queries, after which a timeout error is returned. The default is ’10s'. Riak.conf

title: Configure Riak TS
heading: Timeout#
text: Riak.conf riak_kv.query.timeseries.timeout = 10s

title: Configure Riak TS
heading: Timeout#
text: The supported units for a duration are:

title: Configure Riak TS
heading: Timeout#
text: The supported units for a duration are: Milliseconds - `ms` Seconds - `s` Minutes - `m` Hours - `h` Days - `d` Weeks - `w` Fortnight - `f`

title: Configure Riak TS
heading: Timeout#
text: You can also combine units. For example, setting timeout to 3 minutes and 14 seconds: Riak.conf

title: Configure Riak TS
heading: Timeout#
text: Riak.conf riak_kv.query.timeseries.timeout = 3m14s

title: Configure Riak TS
heading: Timeout#
text: If no unit is added, `riak_kv.query.timeseries.timeout` will be read in milliseconds: Riak.conf

title: Configure Riak TS
heading: Timeout#
text: Riak.conf riak_kv.query.timeseries.timeout = 10000

title: Configure Riak TS
heading: Timeout#
text: This setting was formerly `timeseries_query_timeout_ms`, please update accordingly.

title: Configure Riak TS
heading: Maximum quanta#
text: Note Before you change this setting, we recommend you take a moment to determine whether requantizing your data would be a better option. If your data is not optimally quantized, upping the maximum quanta setting may make your queries less efficient. You can read more about best practices for quantizing your data here.

title: Configure Riak TS
heading: Maximum quanta#
text: If your data is not optimally quantized, upping the maximum quanta setting may make your queries less efficient. You can read more about best practices for quantizing your data here. Use `riak_kv.query.timeseries.max_quanta_span` to configure the maximum number of quanta that a query can span.

title: Configure Riak TS
heading: Maximum quanta#
text: You can read more about best practices for quantizing your data here. Use `riak_kv.query.timeseries.max_quanta_span` to configure the maximum number of quanta that a query can span. The default is 5.

title: Configure Riak TS
heading: Maximum quanta#
text: Use `riak_kv.query.timeseries.max_quanta_span` to configure the maximum number of quanta that a query can span. The default is 5. Riak.conf

title: Configure Riak TS
heading: Maximum quanta#
text: Riak.conf riak_kv.query.timeseries.max_quanta_span = 5

title: Configure Riak TS
heading: Maximum quanta#
text: You should set this parameter to be one more than your desired timespan, else a fraction of your queries will fall outside your `riak_kv.query.timeseries.max_quanta_span` window. In general, your timespan won’t be an integer multiple of the quantum, so if your maximum size query is dtmax, and your quantum size is Q, then we recommend: max_quanta = ceil(dtmax / Q + 1.0). If a query has a larger time span than your specified maximum, the error `too_many_subqueries` will show and the query will not run.

title: Configure Riak TS
heading: Maximum quanta#
text: In general, your timespan won’t be an integer multiple of the quantum, so if your maximum size query is dtmax, and your quantum size is Q, then we recommend: max_quanta = ceil(dtmax / Q + 1.0). If a query has a larger time span than your specified maximum, the error `too_many_subqueries` will show and the query will not run. This option is intended to prevent excessively long-running queries that could affect the performance of the cluster.

title: Configure Riak TS
heading: Maximum quanta#
text: If a query has a larger time span than your specified maximum, the error `too_many_subqueries` will show and the query will not run. This option is intended to prevent excessively long-running queries that could affect the performance of the cluster. The maximum allowable value is 256.

title: Configure Riak TS
heading: Maximum quanta#
text: This option is intended to prevent excessively long-running queries that could affect the performance of the cluster. The maximum allowable value is 256. This setting was formerly `timeseries_query_max_quanta_span`, please update accordingly.

title: Configure Riak TS
heading: Maximum queries#
text: Use `riak_kv.query.timeseries.max_concurrent_queries` to set the maximum number of queries that can run concurrently per node. The default is 3. The total number of queries that can be run on a cluster is the number of nodes multiplied by the `riak_kv.query.timeseries.max_concurrent_queries` value.

title: Configure Riak TS
heading: Maximum queries#
text: The default is 3. The total number of queries that can be run on a cluster is the number of nodes multiplied by the `riak_kv.query.timeseries.max_concurrent_queries` value. This constraint is to prevent an unbounded number of queries overloading the cluster.

title: Configure Riak TS
heading: Maximum queries#
text: The total number of queries that can be run on a cluster is the number of nodes multiplied by the `riak_kv.query.timeseries.max_concurrent_queries` value. This constraint is to prevent an unbounded number of queries overloading the cluster. Riak.conf

title: Configure Riak TS
heading: Maximum queries#
text: Riak.conf riak_kv.query.timeseries.max_concurrent_queries = 3

title: Configure Riak TS
heading: Maximum queries#
text: This setting was formerly `timeseries_max_concurrent_queries`, please update accordingly.

title: Creating and Activating Your Riak TS Table
text: Once you have planned out your table you can create it by:

title: Creating and Activating Your Riak TS Table
text: Once you have planned out your table you can create it by: Executing a CREATE TABLE statement using any Riak TS client, Using riak shell, or Running the `riak-admin` command (as root, using `su` or `sudo`).

title: Creating and Activating Your Riak TS Table
text: Throughout this document, we will again be using the example table: SQL

title: Creating and Activating Your Riak TS Table
text: SQL CREATE TABLE GeoCheckin ( id SINT64 NOT NULL, region VARCHAR NOT NULL, state VARCHAR NOT NULL, time TIMESTAMP NOT NULL, weather VARCHAR NOT NULL, temperature DOUBLE, PRIMARY KEY ( (id, QUANTUM(time, 15, 'm')), id, time ) )

title: Creating and Activating Your Riak TS Table
heading: `CREATE TABLE` in Client Library#
text: Using one of the Riak TS client libraries, execute the CREATE TABLE statement via that library’s query functionality. This will create and activate the table in one step. The result of the operation is library-dependent:

title: Creating and Activating Your Riak TS Table
heading: `CREATE TABLE` in Client Library#
text: The result of the operation is library-dependent: Java: the `QueryResult` object will be returned without any data for rows or columns. Ruby: no exception thrown and result collection is empty. Python: no exception thrown; result object is present with `rows` and `columns` being empty. C#: no exception thrown; result object is present with `Value` and `Columns` being empty. Node.js: no exception thrown; result object is present with `rows` and `columns` being empty. Erlang: the returned term will consist of two empty lists `{[],[]}`. PHP: the response object has a boolean `isSuccess()` instance method.

title: Creating and Activating Your Riak TS Table
heading: Using the WITH clause#
text: Your data definition language (DDL) may have an optional WITH clause, where any table properties can be specified: SQL

title: Creating and Activating Your Riak TS Table
heading: Using the WITH clause#
text: SQL CREATE TABLE (...) WITH ( n_val=5, key2 = 'string value2', prop_with_quotes='single '' quote here', custom_prop = 42.24)

title: Creating and Activating Your Riak TS Table
heading: Using the WITH clause#
text: Please note the following when using `WITH`:

title: Creating and Activating Your Riak TS Table
heading: Using the WITH clause#
text: Please note the following when using `WITH`: The property values can be of numeric or string types (parseable as `sint64`, `double` or `varchar`, correspondingly). String values should be quoted with a `'`; literal single quote characters appearing in the string should be doubled (and not escaped with a `\`). Values from the WITH clause will override those specified outside the query statement.

title: Creating and Activating Your Riak TS Table
heading: Verification via Client Library#
text: You can verify that your table was properly created by executing the DESCRIBE statement via the query function of your client library, or by using the `riak-admin bucket-type status` command.

title: Creating and Activating Your Riak TS Table
heading: Create a table with riak shell#
text: You can use riak shell to create a table by running: Text

title: Creating and Activating Your Riak TS Table
heading: Create a table with riak shell#
text: Text riak-shell>CREATE TABLE GeoCheckin (id SINT64 NOT NULL, region VARCHAR NOT NULL, state VARCHAR NOT NULL, time TIMESTAMP NOT NULL, weather VARCHAR NOT NULL, temperature DOUBLE, PRIMARY KEY ((id, QUANTUM(time, 15, 'm')), id, time));

title: Creating and Activating Your Riak TS Table
heading: Create a table with riak shell#
text: Please take care with the following:

title: Creating and Activating Your Riak TS Table
heading: Create a table with riak shell#
text: Please take care with the following: The syntax is sensitive to whitespace and quoting. The table and column names are currently constrained to ASCII.

title: Creating and Activating Your Riak TS Table
heading: `riak-admin`#
text: To create the example table, first run: (Note: Mac OS X users can skip this step) Bash

title: Creating and Activating Your Riak TS Table
heading: `riak-admin`#
text: Bash sudo su riak

title: Creating and Activating Your Riak TS Table
heading: `riak-admin`#
text: This will put you in a shell as the riak user. Then run: Sh

title: Creating and Activating Your Riak TS Table
heading: `riak-admin`#
text: Sh riak-admin bucket-type create GeoCheckin '{"props":{"table_def": "CREATE TABLE GeoCheckin (id SINT64 NOT NULL, region VARCHAR NOT NULL, state VARCHAR NOT NULL, time TIMESTAMP NOT NULL, weather VARCHAR NOT NULL, temperature DOUBLE, PRIMARY KEY ((id, QUANTUM(time, 15, 'm')), id, time))"}}'

title: Creating and Activating Your Riak TS Table
heading: `riak-admin`#
text: Please take care with the following:

title: Creating and Activating Your Riak TS Table
heading: `riak-admin`#
text: Please take care with the following: The `bucket-type` name must equal the table name. The syntax is very sensitive to whitespace and quoting. It is easy to create a very long bucket type name with no corresponding TS table if you leave out the space between the bucket type name and the opening quote of the JSON properties. The table and column names are currently constrained to ASCII.

title: Creating and Activating Your Riak TS Table
heading: `riak-admin`#
text: Also note that if you discover something wrong with the setup of your data definition language (DDL), you will need to create it again and decide whether to scrap the data in the existing table or move it from the old table to the new one.

title: Creating and Activating Your Riak TS Table
heading: Activating Your Table#
text: You activate your table as follows: Sh

title: Creating and Activating Your Riak TS Table
heading: Activating Your Table#
text: Sh riak-admin bucket-type activate »TABLE NAME«

title: Creating and Activating Your Riak TS Table
heading: Activating Your Table#
text: For the example `GeoCheckin` table: Sh

title: Creating and Activating Your Riak TS Table
heading: Activating Your Table#
text: Sh riak-admin bucket-type activate GeoCheckin

title: Creating and Activating Your Riak TS Table
heading: Verify Creation and Activation#
text: You can verify that your table was properly created by looking at the `ddl` section of the `riak-admin bucket-type status` response. For example: Sh

title: Creating and Activating Your Riak TS Table
heading: Verify Creation and Activation#
text: Sh $ riak-admin bucket-type status GeoCheckin GeoCheckin is active ... ddl: {ddl_v1,<<"GeoCheckin">>, [{riak_field_v1,<<"id">>,1,sint64,false}, {riak_field_v1,<<"region">>,2,varchar,false}, {riak_field_v1,<<"state">>,3,varchar,false}, {riak_field_v1,<<"time">>,4,timestamp,false}, {riak_field_v1,<<"weather">>,5,varchar,false}, {riak_field_v1,<<"temperature">>,6,double,true}], {key_v1,[{param_v1,[<<"id">>]},

title: Creating and Activating Your Riak TS Table
heading: Verify Creation and Activation#
text: {hash_fn_v1,riak_ql_quanta,quantum, [{param_v1,[<<"time">>]},15,m], timestamp}]}, {key_v1,[{param_v1,[<<"id">>]},{param_v1,[<<"time">>]}]}}

title: Creating and Activating Your Riak TS Table
heading: Editing Your Table#
text: Once created, you cannot edit your Riak TS table. If you discover something wrong with the setup of your Riak TS table, you will need to create it again. You will also need to decide whether to scrap the data in the existing table or move it from the old table to the new one.

title: Creating and Activating Your Riak TS Table
heading: Next Steps#
text: Now that you’ve created and activated your Riak TS table, you can write data to it.

title: Configure Global Object Expiration
text: By default, LevelDB keeps all of your data. But Riak TS allows you to configure global object expiration (`expiry`) or time to live (TTL) for your data. Note Currently only global expiration is supported in Riak TS.

title: Configure Global Object Expiration
text: But Riak TS allows you to configure global object expiration (`expiry`) or time to live (TTL) for your data. Note Currently only global expiration is supported in Riak TS. Expiration is disabled by default, but enabling it lets you expire older objects to reclaim the space used or purge data with a limited time value.

title: Configure Global Object Expiration
heading: Enabling Expiry#
text: To enable global object expiry, add the `leveldb.expiration` setting to your riak.conf file: Riak.conf

title: Configure Global Object Expiration
heading: Enabling Expiry#
text: Riak.conf leveldb.expiration = on

title: Configure Global Object Expiration
heading: Enabling Expiry#
text: Note Turning on global object expiration will not retroactively expire previous data. Only data created while expiration is on will be scheduled for expiration.

title: Configure Global Object Expiration
heading: Setting Retention Time#
text: The `retention_time` setting is used to specify the time until objects expire. Durations are set using a combination of an integer and a shortcut for the supported units:

title: Configure Global Object Expiration
heading: Setting Retention Time#
text: Durations are set using a combination of an integer and a shortcut for the supported units: Milliseconds - `ms` Seconds - `s` Minutes - `m` Hours - `h` Days - `d` Weeks - `w` Fortnight - `f`

title: Configure Global Object Expiration
heading: Setting Retention Time#
text: The following example configures objects to expire after 5 hours: Riak.conf

title: Configure Global Object Expiration
heading: Setting Retention Time#
text: Riak.conf leveldb.expiration = on leveldb.expiration.retention_time = 5h

title: Configure Global Object Expiration
heading: Setting Retention Time#
text: You can also combine durations. For example, let’s say you wanted objects to expire after 8 days and 9 hours: Riak.conf

title: Configure Global Object Expiration
heading: Setting Retention Time#
text: Riak.conf leveldb.expiration = on leveldb.expiration.retention_time = 8d9h

title: Configure Global Object Expiration
heading: Expiry Modes#
text: Global expiration supports two modes:

title: Configure Global Object Expiration
heading: Expiry Modes#
text: Global expiration supports two modes: `whole_file` - the whole sorted string table (`.sst`) file is deleted when all of its objects are expired. `normal` - individual objects are removed as part of the usual compaction process.

title: Configure Global Object Expiration
heading: Expiry Modes#
text: We recommend using `whole_file` with time series data that has a similar lifespan, as it will be much more efficient. The following example configure objects to expire after 1 day: Riak.conf

title: Configure Global Object Expiration
heading: Expiry Modes#
text: Riak.conf leveldb.expiration = on leveldb.expiration.retention_time = 1d leveldb.expiration.mode = whole_file

title: Configure Global Object Expiration
heading: Disable Expiry#
text: To disable global object expiration, set `leveldb.expiration` to `off` in your riak.conf file. If expiration is disabled, the other 2 settings are ignored. For example:

title: Configure Global Object Expiration
heading: Disable Expiry#
text: If expiration is disabled, the other 2 settings are ignored. For example: Riak.conf

title: Configure Global Object Expiration
heading: Disable Expiry#
text: Riak.conf leveldb.expiration = off leveldb.expiration.retention_time = 1d leveldb.expiration.mode = whole_file

title: Configure Multi-Datacenter Replication for Riak TS
text: Multi-Datacenter (MDC) replication makes it possible to replicate your time series data between Riak clusters. This document will walk through how to configure MDC to work with Riak TS.

title: Configure Multi-Datacenter Replication for Riak TS
heading: Prerequisites#
text: You must be an Enterprise customer. To contact Basho for information on becoming an Enterprise customer, go here. You must have Riak TS installed on two distinct clusters.

title: Configure Multi-Datacenter Replication for Riak TS
heading: Prerequisites#
text: Warning: Do not attempt to replicate TS data to a Riak cluster on Riak KV or any version of Riak TS prior to 1.3.1.

title: Configure Multi-Datacenter Replication for Riak TS
heading: Prerequisites#
text: Warning: Do not attempt to replicate TS data to a Riak cluster on Riak KV or any version of Riak TS prior to 1.3.1. You must be using Multi-Datacenter v3 (v2 is incompatible with Riak TS). We do not yet support AAE-based fullsync with Riak TS.

title: Configure Multi-Datacenter Replication for Riak TS
heading: MDC#
text: Please see our documentation on basic configuration for MDC. Unlike fullsync, realtime replication can be globally disabled for TS data without impacting the synchronization of Riak KV data. Realtime replication for TS data can be disabled in the `riak_repl` section of your advanced.config file by adding the following setting:

title: Configure Multi-Datacenter Replication for Riak TS
heading: MDC#
text: Unlike fullsync, realtime replication can be globally disabled for TS data without impacting the synchronization of Riak KV data. Realtime replication for TS data can be disabled in the `riak_repl` section of your advanced.config file by adding the following setting: Advanced.config

title: Configure Multi-Datacenter Replication for Riak TS
heading: MDC#
text: Advanced.config {ts_realtime, false}

title: Configure Multi-Datacenter Replication for Riak TS
heading: MDC#
text: Note If `{ts_realtime, false}` is not the last entry in your `riak_repl` configuration block, be sure to add a comma at the end of the line. See below for more granular controls.

title: Configure Multi-Datacenter Replication for Riak TS
heading: TS Tables#
text: Each TS table to be replicated must be defined on each cluster. MDC will not create new tables for you, and will compare the data definition language (DDL) on each cluster to make certain they are equivalent before synchronization occurs.

title: Configure Multi-Datacenter Replication for Riak TS
heading: Turn off replication per-table#
text: In order to disable fullsync, realtime, or all replication for your TS tables, you will need to set the bucket type property `repl` to either `realtime` (to use only realtime sync), `fullsync` (to use only fullsync), or `false`. The default value is `true`, indicating that both realtime and fullsync are enabled. To set the `repl` property to either `true` or `false`, you can use the `riak-admin` command.

title: Configure Multi-Datacenter Replication for Riak TS
heading: Turn off replication per-table#
text: The default value is `true`, indicating that both realtime and fullsync are enabled. To set the `repl` property to either `true` or `false`, you can use the `riak-admin` command. Assuming a table named `sensors`:

title: Configure Multi-Datacenter Replication for Riak TS
heading: Turn off replication per-table#
text: To set the `repl` property to either `true` or `false`, you can use the `riak-admin` command. Assuming a table named `sensors`: Text

title: Configure Multi-Datacenter Replication for Riak TS
heading: Turn off replication per-table#
text: Text $ riak-admin bucket-type update sensors '{"props":{"repl":false}}'

title: Configure Multi-Datacenter Replication for Riak TS
heading: Turn off replication per-table#
text: If you wish to enable only one of the replication modes by setting `repl` to `fullsync` or `realtime`, you must use tweak the properties directly from a Riak node or use a protobuf client. Please contact Basho support for assistance. While replication requires that the TS table be created on both clusters involved, the `repl` property need only be set on a cluster that will be sending data.

title: Planning Your Riak TS Table
heading: TS Table Schema#
text: In order to create a working Riak TS table, you’ll need to plan your table out. Once created, your table cannot be changed. Here is an example Riak TS CREATE TABLE statement (broken across many lines for clarity):

title: Planning Your Riak TS Table
heading: TS Table Schema#
text: Once created, your table cannot be changed. Here is an example Riak TS CREATE TABLE statement (broken across many lines for clarity): SQL

title: Planning Your Riak TS Table

title: Planning Your Riak TS Table
heading: TS Table Schema#
text: A TS table is made up of:

title: Planning Your Riak TS Table
heading: TS Table Schema#
text: A TS table is made up of: a table name, GeoCheckin in this example, column definitions, the first 6 lines after the table name in this example, and the primary key, which is everything following `PRIMARY KEY` in this example.

title: Planning Your Riak TS Table
heading: TS Table Schema#
text: The column definitions will determine the columns of your TS table, while the primary key determines where data is stored in your TS cluster. Keywords are case sensitive, so be sure to capitalize appropriately. Table Limitations You cannot create a table with more than 511 total columns.

title: Planning Your Riak TS Table
heading: TS Table Schema#
text: Keywords are case sensitive, so be sure to capitalize appropriately. Table Limitations You cannot create a table with more than 511 total columns. If you try to create a table with more than 511 columns, you will receive an error.

title: Planning Your Riak TS Table
heading: Column Definitions#
text: Column definitions define the structure of the data and are comprised of three parts: a column name, a data type, and (optionally) an inline constraint. SQL

title: Planning Your Riak TS Table
heading: Column Definitions#
text: SQL column_name data_type [NOT NULL],

title: Planning Your Riak TS Table
heading: Column Definitions#
text: Column names (`region`, `state`, etc) must be ASCII strings, in addition to having the correct case. If column names need to contain spaces or punctuation they can be double quoted. Any column names specified as part of the primary key must be defined as `NOT NULL`.

title: Planning Your Riak TS Table
heading: Column Definitions#
text: If column names need to contain spaces or punctuation they can be double quoted. Any column names specified as part of the primary key must be defined as `NOT NULL`. The column definitions for the keys can be specified in any order in the CREATE TABLE statement.

title: Planning Your Riak TS Table
heading: Column Definitions#
text: The data types in column definitions are limited. Valid types are:

title: Planning Your Riak TS Table
heading: Column Definitions#
text: Valid types are: `VARCHAR` - Any string content is valid, including Unicode. Can only be compared using strict equality, and will not be typecast (e.g., to an integer) for comparison purposes. Use single quotes to delimit varchar strings. `BOOLEAN` - `true` or `false` (any case). `TIMESTAMP` - Integer values expressing UNIX epoch time in UTC in milliseconds. Zero is not a valid timestamp. `SINT64` - Signed 64-bit integer. `DOUBLE` - This type does not comply with its IEEE specification: `NaN` (not a number) and `INF` (infinity) cannot be used.

title: Planning Your Riak TS Table
heading: Primary Key#
text: The `PRIMARY KEY` describes both the partition key and local key. The partition key is a prefix of the local key, consisting of one or more column names in parentheses. The local key must begin with the same column names as the partition key, but may also contain additional column names.

title: Planning Your Riak TS Table
heading: Primary Key#
text: The partition key is a prefix of the local key, consisting of one or more column names in parentheses. The local key must begin with the same column names as the partition key, but may also contain additional column names. SQL

title: Planning Your Riak TS Table
heading: Primary Key#
text: SQL CREATE TABLE GeoCheckin ( region VARCHAR NOT NULL, state VARCHAR NOT NULL, time TIMESTAMP NOT NULL, weather VARCHAR NOT NULL, temperature DOUBLE, PRIMARY KEY ( (region, state, QUANTUM(time, 15, 'm')), <-- PARTITION KEY region, state, time <-- LOCAL KEY ) )

title: Planning Your Riak TS Table
heading: Primary Key#

heading: Primary Key#
text: B. SQL

heading: Primary Key#

title: Planning Your Riak TS Table
heading: Partition Key#
text: The partition key is the first element of the primary key, and must have at least one column name. A general guideline is to first choose a column name that represents a class or type of data, and then choose a second column name that is a more specific instance(s) of the class/type. You may specify a quantum, which is used to colocate data on one of the partition key’s timestamp fields:

title: Planning Your Riak TS Table
heading: Partition Key#
text: A general guideline is to first choose a column name that represents a class or type of data, and then choose a second column name that is a more specific instance(s) of the class/type. You may specify a quantum, which is used to colocate data on one of the partition key’s timestamp fields: SQL

title: Planning Your Riak TS Table
heading: Partition Key#
text: SQL PRIMARY KEY ((region, state, QUANTUM(time, 1, 's')), ...)

title: Planning Your Riak TS Table
heading: Partition Key#
text: If you choose to specify a quantum, you may specify only one and it must be the last element of the partition key. The quantum function takes 3 parameters:

title: Planning Your Riak TS Table
heading: Partition Key#
text: The quantum function takes 3 parameters: the name of a field in the table definition of type `TIMESTAMP` a quantity as a positive integer, greater than zero a unit of time: `'d'` - days `'h'` - hours `'m'` - minutes `'s'` - seconds `'d'` - days `'h'` - hours `'m'` - minutes `'s'` - seconds

title: Planning Your Riak TS Table
heading: Local Key#
text: The local key comes after the partition key. It must first contain the same column names in the same order as the partition key. This ensures that the same column names determining your data’s partition also dictate the sorting of the data within that partition.

title: Planning Your Riak TS Table
heading: Local Key#
text: It must first contain the same column names in the same order as the partition key. This ensures that the same column names determining your data’s partition also dictate the sorting of the data within that partition. The local key may also contain additional column names so long as they come after the column names present in the partition key.

title: Planning Your Riak TS Table
heading: Local Key#
text: This ensures that the same column names determining your data’s partition also dictate the sorting of the data within that partition. The local key may also contain additional column names so long as they come after the column names present in the partition key. For example:

title: Planning Your Riak TS Table
heading: Local Key#

title: Planning Your Riak TS Table
heading: Local Key#
text: SQL PRIMARY KEY ( (region, state, QUANTUM(time, 15, 'm')), region, state, time, weather, temperature )

title: Planning Your Riak TS Table
heading: Local Key#
text: On Key Uniqueness The Local Key in a Riak TS row is what makes that row’s key/address unique from other rows. In the examples on this page and others we’ve used a composite key of `region, state, time` because it can model different devices and groupings. If you have another identifier, such as a device ID, that you can guarantee to be unique when combined with a timestamp, you can have a shorter key definition.

title: Planning Your Riak TS Table
heading: Local Key#
text: In the examples on this page and others we’ve used a composite key of `region, state, time` because it can model different devices and groupings. If you have another identifier, such as a device ID, that you can guarantee to be unique when combined with a timestamp, you can have a shorter key definition.

title: Planning Your Riak TS Table
heading: Local Key#
text: The table definition for such a schema would be as follows: SQL CREATE TABLE GeoCheckin ( id SINT64 NOT NULL, region VARCHAR NOT NULL, state VARCHAR NOT NULL, time TIMESTAMP NOT NULL, weather VARCHAR NOT NULL, temperature DOUBLE, PRIMARY KEY ( (id, QUANTUM(time, 15, 'm')), <-- PARTITION KEY id, time <-- LOCAL KEY ) ) The omission of `region` and `state` from the key definition makes it shorter, and will also make any SQL queries shorter because we’ll only need a minimum of id/time in our queries `WHERE` clauses (see Table Architecture and Querying Guidelines for all the specifics about how different partition + local key layouts change the way you query data).

title: Planning Your Riak TS Table
heading: Local Key#
text: If you have another identifier, such as a device ID, that you can guarantee to be unique when combined with a timestamp, you can have a shorter key definition. The table definition for such a schema would be as follows: SQL CREATE TABLE GeoCheckin ( id SINT64 NOT NULL, region VARCHAR NOT NULL, state VARCHAR NOT NULL, time TIMESTAMP NOT NULL, weather VARCHAR NOT NULL, temperature DOUBLE, PRIMARY KEY ( (id, QUANTUM(time, 15, 'm')), <-- PARTITION KEY id, time <-- LOCAL KEY ) ) The omission of `region` and `state` from the key definition makes it shorter, and will also make any SQL queries shorter because we’ll only need a minimum of id/time in our queries `WHERE` clauses (see Table Architecture and Querying Guidelines for all the specifics about how different partition + local key layouts change the way you query data).

title: Planning Your Riak TS Table
heading: Local Key#
text: The downside to this schema is that you’ll likely need to do one query per device, instead of being able to group multiple devices together based on their other defining characteristics such as region & state.

title: Planning Your Riak TS Table
heading: Local Key#
text: The table definition for such a schema would be as follows: SQL CREATE TABLE GeoCheckin ( id SINT64 NOT NULL, region VARCHAR NOT NULL, state VARCHAR NOT NULL, time TIMESTAMP NOT NULL, weather VARCHAR NOT NULL, temperature DOUBLE, PRIMARY KEY ( (id, QUANTUM(time, 15, 'm')), <-- PARTITION KEY id, time <-- LOCAL KEY ) ) The omission of `region` and `state` from the key definition makes it shorter, and will also make any SQL queries shorter because we’ll only need a minimum of id/time in our queries `WHERE` clauses (see Table Architecture and Querying Guidelines for all the specifics about how different partition + local key layouts change the way you query data). The downside to this schema is that you’ll likely need to do one query per device, instead of being able to group multiple devices together based on their other defining characteristics such as region & state. Please take care in defining how you address your unique data, as it will affect how you will query it in the future.

title: DESCRIBE in Riak TS
text: You can use the DESCRIBE statement to obtain the definition of your Riak TS table. This document will show you how to execute `DESCRIBE` in TS. The DESCRIBE statement returns the table’s information in rows and columns.

title: DESCRIBE in Riak TS

title: DESCRIBE in Riak TS
text: Using TS’s supported clients, a successful `DESCRIBE` will return a language-specific representation of the table. Java - Use a `Query` command to execute a DESCRIBE statement. Ruby - Use the `Riak::TimeSeries::Query` object to execute the DESCRIBE statement. The returned results will have a collection of rows as well as a `columns` property corresponding to the above table. Python - either the `ts_query` or `ts_describe` methods of the client object can be used to executed a DESCRIBE statement. In both cases, the response object will have `columns` and `rows` properties corresponding to the above table. C# - Use a `Query` command to execute a DESCRIBE statement. In both cases, the response object will have `columns` and `rows` properties corresponding to the above table.

title: EXPLAIN in Riak TS
text: You can use the EXPLAIN statement to better understand how a query you would like to run will be executed. This document will show you how to use `EXPLAIN` in Riak TS.

title: EXPLAIN in Riak TS
heading: EXPLAIN Guidelines#
text: `EXPLAIN` takes a SELECT statement as an argument and shows information about each subquery. The constraints placed upon the WHERE clause in the SELECT statement determine the subquery values. The details about each subquery include:

title: EXPLAIN in Riak TS
heading: EXPLAIN Guidelines#
text: The details about each subquery include: A subquery number which is a unique integer, The range scan start key which shows the value of the fields at the beginning of that quantum, A flag indicating if that flag is inclusive (less than or greater than or equal), The range scan end key, Another inclusive flag for the end key, and The value of the filter, i.e. constrained columns which are not a part of the partition key

title: EXPLAIN in Riak TS
heading: EXPLAIN Guidelines#
text: To use `EXPLAIN`, the table in question must first be defined and activated. Only metadata about the desired query is returned.

title: EXPLAIN in Riak TS
heading: EXPLAIN Example#
text: Assuming our standard example table, GeoCheckin, has been created: SQL

title: EXPLAIN in Riak TS
heading: EXPLAIN Example#
text: SQL CREATE TABLE GeoCheckin ( region VARCHAR NOT NULL, state VARCHAR NOT NULL, time TIMESTAMP NOT NULL, weather VARCHAR NOT NULL, temperature DOUBLE, PRIMARY KEY ( (region, state, QUANTUM(time, 15, 'm')), region, state, time ) )

title: Guidelines for Querying in Riak TS
text: Riak TS supports several kinds of queries of your TS data. To create the most successful queries possible, there are some guidelines and limitations you should know. This document will cover the basic rules of querying in Riak TS, general guidelines to help you create the best queries possible, and all current limitations impacting queries in TS.

title: Guidelines for Querying in Riak TS
heading: The Basic Rules of Querying#
text: You query data via columns. There are three categories of column, each with a different set of rules for valid queries. Query columns are based on rows in your TS table.

title: Guidelines for Querying in Riak TS
heading: The Basic Rules of Querying#
text: There are three categories of column, each with a different set of rules for valid queries. Query columns are based on rows in your TS table. Text

title: Guidelines for Querying in Riak TS
heading: The Basic Rules of Querying#
text: Text CREATE TABLE tab2( a SINT64 NOT NULL, b TIMESTAMP NOT NULL, c BOOLEAN NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY ((a, QUANTUM(b, 1, 's'))<-Partition Key, a,b,c)<-Local Key)

title: Guidelines for Querying in Riak TS
heading: Partition Key#
text: Text

title: Guidelines for Querying in Riak TS
heading: Partition Key#
text: Text PRIMARY KEY ((a,<-Unquantized QUANTUM(b, 1, 's')<-Quantized)...

title: Guidelines for Querying in Riak TS
heading: Partition Key#
text: All queries must cover the partition key fields and must use greater than and less than (>, >=, <, <=). All unquantized fields in your partition key must be included in the query as exact matches. Any quantized field in your partition key must be included in the query as either an exact match or a bounded range.

title: Guidelines for Querying in Riak TS
heading: Partition Key#
text: Any quantized field in your partition key must be included in the query as either an exact match or a bounded range. Valid: `time > 1449864277000 and time < 1449864290000` Invalid: `time > 1449864277000` Invalid: `time > 1449864277000 or time < 1449864290000`

title: Guidelines for Querying in Riak TS
heading: Partition Key#
text: A Note About `SELECT` It is possible to use ISO 8601-compliant date/time strings rather than integer timestamps in SELECT statements. Please see SELECT for an example or Time Representations for more information.

title: Guidelines for Querying in Riak TS
heading: Local Key#
text: For any field in the local key that is not in the partition key, your query can include any operator supported for that field’s type. Bounded ranges are not required. Text

title: Guidelines for Querying in Riak TS
heading: Local Key#
text: Text PRIMARY KEY ((a,b),a,b,c)

title: Guidelines for Querying in Riak TS
heading: Local Key#
text: Here ‘c’ is in the local key only so does not have to be in the query. Column names from the local key must be compared using strict equality against literal values. No ranges are permitted, `!=` must not be used, and `or` will not work.

title: Guidelines for Querying in Riak TS
heading: Local Key#
text: No ranges are permitted, `!=` must not be used, and `or` will not work. Valid: `country_code = 'uk'` Invalid: `(country_code = 'uk' or country_code = 'de')` Invalid: `country_code != 'se'` Invalid: `temperature < 85.0`

title: Guidelines for Querying in Riak TS
heading: Column Definitions#
text: Column definitions may be queried with unbounded ranges, `!=`, and `or` comparisons.

title: Guidelines for Querying in Riak TS
heading: General Guidelines#
text: Before you begin querying, there are some guidelines to keep in mind.

title: Guidelines for Querying in Riak TS
heading: General Guidelines#
text: Before you begin querying, there are some guidelines to keep in mind. Columns may not be compared against other columns in the query. When using `or`, you must surround the expression with parentheses or your query will return an error.

title: Guidelines for Querying in Riak TS
heading: General Guidelines#
text: Basic queries return the full range of values between two given times for an instance within a class or type of data. In the example table, `state` is an instance within the `region`: SQL

title: Guidelines for Querying in Riak TS
heading: General Guidelines#
text: SQL CREATE TABLE GeoCheckin ( region VARCHAR NOT NULL, state VARCHAR NOT NULL, time TIMESTAMP NOT NULL, weather VARCHAR NOT NULL, temperature DOUBLE, PRIMARY KEY ( (region, state, QUANTUM(time, 15, 'm')), region, state, time ) )

title: Guidelines for Querying in Riak TS
heading: General Guidelines#
text: Your query must include all components of the partition key. If any part of the partition key is missing, you will get an error.

title: Guidelines for Querying in Riak TS
heading: SQL Support#
text: A small subset of SQL is supported. All columns are of the format: SQL

title: Guidelines for Querying in Riak TS
heading: SQL Support#
text: SQL Field Operator Constant

title: Guidelines for Querying in Riak TS
heading: SQL Support#
text: The following operators are supported for each data type:

title: Guidelines for Querying in Riak TS
heading: SQL Support#
text: The following operators are supported for each data type: = != > < <= >= varchar X X boolean X X sint64 X X X X X X double X X X X X X timestamp X X X X X X

title: Guidelines for Querying in Riak TS
heading: Limitations#
text: Column to column comparisons are not currently supported. Secondary indexing (2i) will not work with Riak TS. Riak Search will not work with Riak TS. Queries are limited by the number of quanta they can span when specifying the time limits.

title: Guidelines for Querying in Riak TS
heading: Quanta query range#
text: A query covering more than a certain number of quanta (5 by default) will generate the error `too_many_subqueries` and the query system will refuse to run it. Assuming a default quantum of 15 minutes, the maximum query time range is 75 minutes. In the below example we set a quantum of 15s:

title: Guidelines for Querying in Riak TS
heading: Quanta query range#
text: Assuming a default quantum of 15 minutes, the maximum query time range is 75 minutes. In the below example we set a quantum of 15s: SQL

title: Guidelines for Querying in Riak TS
heading: Quanta query range#
text: SQL CREATE TABLE GeoCheckin (geohash VARCHAR NOT NULL, location VARCHAR NOT NULL, user VARCHAR NOT NULL, time TIMESTAMP NOT NULL, weather VARCHAR NOT NULL, temperature VARCHAR, PRIMARY KEY((location, user, QUANTUM(time, 15, 's')), location, user, time))

title: Guidelines for Querying in Riak TS
heading: Quanta query range#
text: The maximum time range we can query is 60s, anything beyond will fail. See the Data Modeling section in Table Architecture for more information.

title: Guidelines for Querying in Riak TS
heading: Leap seconds and quantum boundaries#
text: Periodically leap seconds are announced. These are inserted at the end of one day (in UTC). UNIX treats them as one double-length second.

title: Guidelines for Querying in Riak TS
heading: Leap seconds and quantum boundaries#
text: These are inserted at the end of one day (in UTC). UNIX treats them as one double-length second. For example, at the end of 1998 a second was added:

title: Guidelines for Querying in Riak TS
heading: Leap seconds and quantum boundaries#
text: UNIX treats them as one double-length second. For example, at the end of 1998 a second was added: Text

title: Guidelines for Querying in Riak TS
heading: Leap seconds and quantum boundaries#

title: Guidelines for Querying in Riak TS
heading: Leap seconds and quantum boundaries#
text: Effectively, there is no way in the UNIX time scheme to differentiate an event that occurred during the extra second at the end of 1998 to something that occurred the first second of 1999. Similarly, Riak TS would treat `915148800` as the start of a new time quantum, and any data points which a client added for that second would be considered to be in the first time quantum in 1999. The data is not lost, but a query against 1998 time quanta will not produce those data points despite the fact that some of the events flagged as `915148800` technically occurred in 1998.

title: Riak TS Aggregate Functions
text: You can turn a set of rows in your Riak TS table into a value with the aggregate feature. This document will walk you through the functions that make up aggregation in Riak TS.

title: Riak TS Aggregate Functions
heading: Aggregate Functions#
text: `COUNT()` - Returns the number of entries that match a specified criteria. `SUM()` - Returns the sum of entries that match a specified criteria. `MEAN()` & `AVG()` - Returns the average of entries that match a specified criteria. `MIN()` - Returns the smallest value of entries that match a specified criteria. `MAX()` - Returns the largest value of entries that match a specified criteria. `STDDEV()`/`STDDEV_SAMP()` - Returns the statistical standard deviation of all entries that match a specified criteria using Sample Standard Deviation. `STDDEV_POP()` - Returns the statistical standard deviation of all entries that match a specified criteria using Population Standard Deviation.

title: Riak TS Aggregate Functions
heading: Aggregate Functions#
text: A Note On Negation You cannot negate an aggregate function. If you attempt something like: `select -count(temperature)`, you will receive an error. Instead, you can achieve negation with `-1*`; for instance: `-1*COUNT(...)`.

title: GROUP BY in Riak TS
text: The GROUP BY statement is used with `SELECT` to pick out and condense rows sharing the same value and return a single row. `GROUP BY` is useful for aggregating an attribute of a device over a time period; for instance, you could use it to pull average values for every 30 minute period over the last 24 hours. This document will show you how to run various queries using `GROUP BY`. See the guidelines for more information on limitations and rules for queries in TS.

title: GROUP BY in Riak TS
heading: GROUP BY Basics#
text: `GROUP BY` returns a single row for each unique combination of values for columns specified in the GROUP BY statement. There is no guaranteed order for the returned rows. The SELECT statement must contain only the columns specified in `GROUP BY`.

title: GROUP BY in Riak TS
heading: GROUP BY Basics#
text: There is no guaranteed order for the returned rows. The SELECT statement must contain only the columns specified in `GROUP BY`. Columns not used as groups can appear as function parameters.

title: GROUP BY in Riak TS
heading: GROUP BY Basics#
text: The SELECT statement must contain only the columns specified in `GROUP BY`. Columns not used as groups can appear as function parameters. The GROUP BY statement works on all rows, not just the values in the partition key, so all columns are available.

title: GROUP BY in Riak TS
heading: GROUP BY Basics#
text: Columns not used as groups can appear as function parameters. The GROUP BY statement works on all rows, not just the values in the partition key, so all columns are available. The aggregate function may be used with the GROUP BY statement.

title: GROUP BY in Riak TS
heading: GROUP BY Basics#
text: The GROUP BY statement works on all rows, not just the values in the partition key, so all columns are available. The aggregate function may be used with the GROUP BY statement. If used, `SELECT` may contain the columns specified in either `GROUP BY` or the aggregate function.

title: GROUP BY in Riak TS
heading: GROUP BY Basics#
text: The aggregate function may be used with the GROUP BY statement. If used, `SELECT` may contain the columns specified in either `GROUP BY` or the aggregate function. WARNING Before you run `GROUP BY` you must ensure the node issuing the query has adequate memory to receive the response.

title: GROUP BY in Riak TS
heading: GROUP BY Basics#
text: If used, `SELECT` may contain the columns specified in either `GROUP BY` or the aggregate function. WARNING Before you run `GROUP BY` you must ensure the node issuing the query has adequate memory to receive the response. If the returning rows do not fit into the memory of the requesting node, the node is likely to fail.

title: GROUP BY in Riak TS
heading: GROUP BY Examples#
text: The following table defines a schema for tasks, including which project they are part of and when they were completed. SQL

title: GROUP BY in Riak TS
heading: GROUP BY Examples#
text: SQL CREATE TABLE tasks ( name VARCHAR NOT NULL, project VARCHAR NOT NULL, completed TIMESTAMP NOT NULL, subtask VARCHAR NOT NULL, duration SINT64 NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY((name,project,quantum(completed,1,'m')),name,project,completed) );

title: GROUP BY in Riak TS
heading: Basic GROUP BY#
text: The query below returns one column per unique project and counts how many rows have the same project. SQL

title: GROUP BY in Riak TS
heading: Basic GROUP BY#
text: SQL SELECT project, COUNT(name) FROM tasks WHERE completed > 1 AND completed < 1000 AND name = 'wheels' AND project = 'Mars Rover' GROUP BY project;

title: GROUP BY in Riak TS
heading: More than one group#
text: You can group as many columns as you choose, and the order of the grouping has no effect. The query below returns one column per unique project, name combination, and counts how many rows have the same project, name combination. SQL

title: GROUP BY in Riak TS
heading: More than one group#
text: SQL SELECT project, COUNT(name) FROM tasks WHERE completed > 1 AND completed < 1000 AND name = 'wheels' AND project = 'Mars Rover' GROUP BY project, name;

title: GROUP BY in Riak TS
heading: Timestamps in a group#
text: Warning Using a timestamp in the group can produce large number of groups due to the likelihood of the timestamps being unique. You can include the timestamp (or quantized column) in the group. The query below returns one column per unique project, name, timestamp combination.

title: GROUP BY in Riak TS
heading: Timestamps in a group#
text: You can include the timestamp (or quantized column) in the group. The query below returns one column per unique project, name, timestamp combination. SQL

title: GROUP BY in Riak TS
heading: Timestamps in a group#
text: SQL SELECT project, name, completed FROM tasks WHERE completed > 1 AND completed < 1000 AND name = 'wheels' AND project = 'Mars Rover' GROUP BY project, name, completed;

title: GROUP BY in Riak TS
heading: Using combination aggregate functions#
text: If you use a combination aggregate function (`COUNT()`, `SUM()`, `MEAN()`, `AVG()`, `STDDEV()`, `STDDEV_SAMP()`, and `STDDEV_POP()`) with the SELECT statement, you can specify the column in the aggregate function alone, or in both the `SELECT` and the aggregate function. This is allowed because the values returned can be grouped into one value: the result of the COUNT function. The query below returns one column per unique project, name combination and counts how many rows have the same name.

title: GROUP BY in Riak TS
heading: Using combination aggregate functions#
text: This is allowed because the values returned can be grouped into one value: the result of the COUNT function. The query below returns one column per unique project, name combination and counts how many rows have the same name. SQL

title: GROUP BY in Riak TS
heading: Using combination aggregate functions#
text: SQL SELECT COUNT(name) FROM tasks WHERE completed > 1 AND completed < 1000 AND name = 'wheels' AND project = 'Mars Rover' GROUP BY project, name;

title: GROUP BY in Riak TS
heading: Using combination aggregate functions#
text: The query below returns one column per unique project and counts how many rows have the same timestamp. SQL

title: GROUP BY in Riak TS
heading: Using combination aggregate functions#
text: SQL SELECT project, COUNT(completed) FROM tasks WHERE completed > 1 AND completed < 1000 AND name = 'wheels' AND project = 'Mars Rover' GROUP BY project;

title: GROUP BY in Riak TS
heading: GROUP BY columns not in the partition key#
text: Since the GROUP BY statement works on all rows, all columns are available, which means that using `GROUP BY` on the partition key values is not very useful because the partition key limits the result set. If we create the following table: SQL

title: GROUP BY in Riak TS
heading: GROUP BY columns not in the partition key#
text: SQL CREATE TABLE tasks2 ( userid VARCHAR NOT NULL, visits SINT64, a_time TIMESTAMP NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY(userid, a_time));

title: GROUP BY in Riak TS
heading: GROUP BY columns not in the partition key#
text: And and try to run the GROUP BY statement including `userid` in the SELECT statement: SQL

title: GROUP BY in Riak TS
heading: GROUP BY columns not in the partition key#
text: SQL SELECT userid, SUM(visits) FROM tasks2 WHERE userid = 'roddy' AND a_time > 1 AND a_time < 10000 GROUP BY userid;

title: GROUP BY in Riak TS
heading: GROUP BY columns not in the partition key#
text: The result set would only have the group ‘roddy’ because it is required by the WHERE clause. If, however, we combine two column names from the partition key in the group using `SUM` without specifying `userid`, `GROUP BY` will return multiple result rows for the `userid` ‘roddy’ with one column per visit.

text: Java final List<Cell> keyCells = Arrays.asList(new Cell("South Atlantic"), new Cell("South Carolina"), Cell.newTimestamp(1420113600000)); Fetch fetch = new Fetch.Builder("GeoCheckin", keyCells).build(); QueryResult queryResult = client.execute(fetch);

text: Text riak-shell>CREATE TABLE GeoCheckin (region VARCHAR NOT NULL, state VARCHAR NOT NULL, time TIMESTAMP NOT NULL, weather VARCHAR NOT NULL, temperature DOUBLE, PRIMARY KEY ((region, state, QUANTUM(time, 15, 'm')), region, state, time));

title: Using riak shell
heading: SQL#
text: Then, you can see the table in riak shell: Text

title: Using riak shell
heading: SQL#
text: Text riak-shell>describe GeoCheckin; +-----------+---------+-------+-----------+---------+ | Column | Type |Is Null|Primary Key|Local Key| +-----------+---------+-------+-----------+---------+ | region | varchar | false | 1 | 1 | | state | varchar | false | 2 | 2 | | time |timestamp| false | 3 | 3 | | weather | varchar | false | | | |temperature| double | true | | | +-----------+---------+-------+-----------+---------+

title: Using riak shell
heading: SQL#
text: You can also select specific data points from your table: Text

title: Using riak shell
heading: SQL#
text: Text riak-shell(28)>SELECT time, weather, temperature FROM GeoCheckin WHERE myfamily='family1' AND myseries='series1' AND time > 0 AND time < 1000; +------------------------+-------+--------------------------+ | time |weather| temperature | +------------------------+-------+--------------------------+ |1970-01-01T00:00:00.001Z| snow |2.51999999999999992895e+01|

title: Using riak shell
heading: SQL#
text: You can add data via a simple SQL INSERT statement, too: SQL

title: Using riak shell
heading: SQL#
text: SQL riak-shell>INSERT INTO GeoCheckin (region, state, time, weather, temperature) VALUES ('South Atlantic','South Carolina',1420113600000,'snow',25.2);

title: Using riak shell
heading: SQL#
text: See Writing Data for more details. Note SQL commands in riak shell may span multiple lines.
