title: Using riak shell
heading: Configuration#
text: You can configure riak shell from the riak_shell.config file. You can find the file in your Riak TS directory. The following things can be configured:

title: Using riak shell
heading: Configuration#
text: The following things can be configured: `logging` (on | off) - Defaults to ‘off’; determines whether or not to enable logging. `date_log` (on | off) - Defaults to ‘off’; determines whether or not to add timestamp information to the logs. `logfile` ("../some/dir/mylogfile.log") - Defaults to ‘../log/riak_shell.log’; sets the name and location of the logfile. `cookie` - No default; any atom representing the Erlang cookie that riak shell uses to connect to Riak. `show_connection_status` (true | false) - Defaults to ‘false’; sets whether to show the green tick or red cross in the command line. `nodes` ([nodenames]) - No defaults; a list of nodes to try and connect to on startup or ‘reconnect;’.

title: Checklist
text: Before turning on Riak TS security there are key steps all applications need to take. Missing one of these steps may break your application, so make sure you have done each of the following BEFORE enabling security:

title: Checklist
text: Missing one of these steps may break your application, so make sure you have done each of the following BEFORE enabling security: Because Riak TS security requires a secure SSL connection, you will need to generate appropriate SSL certs, enable SSL and establish a certification configuration on each node. If you enable security without having established a functioning SSL connection, all requests to Riak TS will fail. Define users and, optionally, groups Define an authentication source for each user Grant the necessary permissions to each user (and/or group) Make sure that your client software will work properly: It must pass authentication information with each request It must support encrypted Protocol Buffers traffic It must pass authentication information with each request It must support encrypted Protocol Buffers traffic If you have applications that rely on an already existing Riak TS cluster, make sure that those applications are prepared to gracefully transition into using Riak security once security is enabled.

title: Checklist
text: After all of the above steps have been performed and your security setup has been properly checked, visit the Riak TS Security: Enabling page for instructions on enabling security.

title: Enable & Disable
text: Riak TS security may be checked, enabled, or disabled through the command line, allowing an administrator to change security settings for the whole cluster without needing to go node-by-node.

title: Enable & Disable
heading: Enabling SSL#
text: SSL is disabled by default. In order to use any authentication or authorization features, you must enable SSL for Riak TS. Enabling SSL on a given node requires you to specify a host and port for the node:

title: Enable & Disable
heading: Enabling SSL#
text: In order to use any authentication or authorization features, you must enable SSL for Riak TS. Enabling SSL on a given node requires you to specify a host and port for the node: Riak.conf

title: Enable & Disable
heading: Enabling SSL#
text: Riak.conf listener.protobuf.$name = {"127.0.0.1",8087}

title: Enable & Disable
heading: Enabling Security#
text: Warning: Enable security with caution Enabling security will change the way your client libraries and your applications interact with Riak TS. Once security is enabled, all client connections must be encrypted and all permissions will be denied by default. Do not enable this in production until you have worked through the security checklist and tested everything in a non-production environment.

title: Enable & Disable
heading: Enabling Security#
text: Once security is enabled, all client connections must be encrypted and all permissions will be denied by default. Do not enable this in production until you have worked through the security checklist and tested everything in a non-production environment. Riak TS security is disabled by default.

title: Enable & Disable
heading: Enabling Security#
text: Do not enable this in production until you have worked through the security checklist and tested everything in a non-production environment. Riak TS security is disabled by default. To enable it:

title: Enable & Disable
heading: Enabling Security#
text: Riak TS security is disabled by default. To enable it: Bash

title: Enable & Disable
heading: Enabling Security#
text: Bash riak-admin security enable

title: Enable & Disable
heading: Enabling Security#
text: All users, groups, authentication sources, and permissions can be configured while security is disabled. This lets you create a security configuration without prematurely impacting the service. Keep this in mind when you are managing users and managing sources.

title: Enable & Disable
heading: Disabling Security#
text: If you disable security, all of the various permissions checks that take place when executing operations against Riak TS will be disabled. Users, groups, and other security attributes remain available for configuration while security is disabled, and will be applied if and when security is re-enabled. Bash

title: Enable & Disable
heading: Disabling Security#
text: Bash riak-admin security disable

title: Enable & Disable
heading: Disabling Security#
text: While security is disabled, clients will need to be reconfigured to no longer require TLS and send credentials.

title: Enable & Disable
heading: Checking Security Status#
text: To check whether security is currently enabled for the cluster, use the `status` command: Bash

title: Enable & Disable
heading: Checking Security Status#
text: Bash riak-admin security status

title: Enable & Disable
heading: Checking Security Status#
text: This command will return `Enabled` or `Disabled`.

title: Notifying Riak
text: Data security is an important and sensitive issue. A real-world approach to security allows us to balance appropriate levels of security and related overhead while creating a fast, scalable, and operationally straightforward database.

title: Notifying Riak
heading: Continuous Improvement#
text: Though we make every effort to thwart security vulnerabilities whenever possible, no system is completely secure. We will never claim that Riak is 100% secure (and you should seriously doubt anyone who claims their solution is). What we can promise is that we openly accept all vulnerabilities from the community.

title: Notifying Riak
heading: Continuous Improvement#
text: We will never claim that Riak is 100% secure (and you should seriously doubt anyone who claims their solution is). What we can promise is that we openly accept all vulnerabilities from the community. When appropriate, we’ll publish and make every attempt to quickly address these concerns.

title: Notifying Riak
heading: Balance#
text: More layers of security increase operational and administrative costs. Sometimes those costs are warranted, sometimes they are not. Our approach is to strike an appropriate balance between effort, cost, and security.

title: Notifying Riak
heading: Balance#
text: Sometimes those costs are warranted, sometimes they are not. Our approach is to strike an appropriate balance between effort, cost, and security. For example, Riak does not have fine-grained role-base security.

title: Notifying Riak
heading: Balance#
text: Our approach is to strike an appropriate balance between effort, cost, and security. For example, Riak does not have fine-grained role-base security. Though it can be an attractive bullet-point in a database comparison chart, you’re usually better off finely controlling data access through your application or a service layer.

title: Notifying Riak
heading: Contact Riak#
text: If you discover a potential security issue, please please email us, and allow us 48 hours to reply. We appreciate the effort of the community working with us to create the most secure solution we can. This allows us to open a dialogue with the security community on how best to handle a possible exploit without putting any users at risk.

title: Sources Management
text: While user management enables you to control user authorization, security sources provide an interface for managing means of authentication. If you create users and grant them access to some or all of Riak TS’s functionality as described in the User Management section, you will need to define security sources required for authentication.

title: Sources Management
heading: Available Sources#
text: There are four available authentication sources in Riak TS Security:

title: Sources Management
heading: Available Sources#
text: There are four available authentication sources in Riak TS Security: Source Description trusted networks (`trust`) Always authenticate successfully if access has been granted to a user or all users on the specified CIDR range password (`password`) Check the user’s password against the PBKFD2-hashed password stored in Riak TS pluggable authentication modules (PAM) (`pam`) Authenticate against the given pluggable authentication module (PAM) service certificates (`certificate`) Authenticate using a client certificate

title: Sources Management
heading: Add a Source#
text: Riak TS security sources may be applied to a specific user, multiple users, or all users (`all`). In general, the `add-source` command takes the following form: Bash

title: Sources Management
heading: Add a Source#
text: Bash riak-admin security add-source all|<users> <CIDR> <source> [<option>=<value>[...]]

title: Sources Management
heading: Add a Source#
text: Using `all` indicates that the authentication source can be added to all users. A source can be added to a specific user, for example `add-source superuser`, or to a list of users separated by commas, for example `add-source jane,bill,admin`. The examples in the following sections will assume that the network in question is `127.0.0.1/32` and that a Riak TS user named `riakuser` has been created and that security has been enabled.

title: Sources Management
heading: Trust-based Authentication#
text: This form of authentication (`trust`) enables you to specify trusted CIDRs from which all clients will be authenticated by default. Let’s say that we want to give all users trusted access to securables (without a password) when requests come from `localhost`: Bash

title: Sources Management
heading: Trust-based Authentication#
text: Bash riak-admin security add-source all 127.0.0.1/32 trust

title: Sources Management
heading: Trust-based Authentication#
text: At that point, the `riak-admin security print-sources` command would print the following: Text

title: Sources Management
heading: Trust-based Authentication#
text: You can also specify users as trusted users, as in the following example: Bash

title: Sources Management
heading: Trust-based Authentication#
text: Bash riak-admin security add-source riakuser 127.0.0.1/32 trust

title: Sources Management
heading: Trust-based Authentication#
text: Now, `riakuser` can interact with Riak TS without providing credentials. Running the `riak-admin security print-sources` command would print: Text

title: Sources Management
heading: Password-based Authentication#
text: Authenticating with the `password` source requires that our `riakuser` be given a password. `riakuser` can be assigned a password upon creation, as in this example: Bash

title: Sources Management
heading: Password-based Authentication#
text: Bash riak-admin security add-user riakuser password=captheorem4life

title: Sources Management
heading: Password-based Authentication#
text: Or a password can be assigned to an already existing user by modifying that user’s characteristics: Bash

title: Sources Management
heading: Password-based Authentication#
text: Bash riak-admin security alter-user riakuser password=captheorem4life

title: Sources Management
heading: Password-based Authentication#
text: Running the `riak-admin security print-sources` command would print: Text

title: Sources Management
heading: Password-based Authentication#
text: You can specify that all users must authenticate themselves via password when connecting to Riak from `localhost`: Bash

title: Sources Management
heading: Password-based Authentication#
text: Bash riak-admin security add-source all 127.0.0.1/32 password

title: Sources Management
heading: Password-based Authentication#
text: Or you can specify that any number of specific users must do so: Bash

title: Sources Management
heading: Password-based Authentication#
text: Bash riak-admin security add-source riakuser 127.0.0.1/32 password riak-admin security add-source otheruser 127.0.0.1/32 password

title: Sources Management
heading: Password-based Authentication#
text: Now, our `riakuser` must enter a username and password to have any access to Riak TS. We can check this by using the `riak-admin security print-sources` command: Text

title: Sources Management
heading: Certificate-based Authentication#
text: This form of authentication (`certificate`) requires that Riak TS and a specified client (or clients) interacting with Riak TS have certificates signed by the same Root Certificate Authority. Let’s specify that our user `riakuser` is going to be authenticated using a certificate on `localhost`: Bash

title: Sources Management
heading: Certificate-based Authentication#
text: Bash riak-admin security add-source riakuser 127.0.0.1/32 certificate

title: Sources Management
heading: Certificate-based Authentication#
text: When the `certificate` source is used, `riakuser` must also be entered as the common name, aka `CN`, that you specified when you generated your certificate, as in the following OpenSSL example: Bash

title: Sources Management
heading: Certificate-based Authentication#
text: Bash openssl req -new ... '/CN=riakuser'

title: Sources Management
heading: Certificate-based Authentication#
text: You can add a `certificate` source to any number of clients, as long as their `CN` and Riak TS username match. On the server side, you need to configure Riak TS by specifying a path to your certificates. First, copy all relevant files to your Riak TS cluster.

title: Sources Management
heading: Certificate-based Authentication#
text: On the server side, you need to configure Riak TS by specifying a path to your certificates. First, copy all relevant files to your Riak TS cluster. The default directory for certificates is `/etc`.

title: Sources Management
heading: Certificate-based Authentication#
text: First, copy all relevant files to your Riak TS cluster. The default directory for certificates is `/etc`. You can specify a different directory in your `riak.conf` by either uncommenting those lines (if you choose to use the defaults) or setting the paths yourself:

title: Sources Management
heading: Certificate-based Authentication#
text: The default directory for certificates is `/etc`. You can specify a different directory in your `riak.conf` by either uncommenting those lines (if you choose to use the defaults) or setting the paths yourself: Riak.conf

title: Sources Management
heading: Certificate-based Authentication#
text: Riak.conf ssl.certfile = /path/to/cert.pem ssl.keyfile = /path/to/key.pem ssl.cacertfile = /path/to/cacert.pem

title: Sources Management
heading: Certificate-based Authentication#
text: In the client-side example above, the client’s `CN` and Riak TS username needed to match. On the server (i.e. Riak TS) side, the `CN` specified on each node must match the node’s name as registered by Riak TS. You can find the node’s name in `riak.conf` under the parameter `nodename`.

title: Sources Management
heading: Certificate-based Authentication#
text: On the server (i.e. Riak TS) side, the `CN` specified on each node must match the node’s name as registered by Riak TS. You can find the node’s name in `riak.conf` under the parameter `nodename`. And so if the `nodename` for a cluster is `riakts-node-1`, you would need to generate your certificate with that in mind, as in this OpenSSL example:

title: Sources Management
heading: Certificate-based Authentication#
text: You can find the node’s name in `riak.conf` under the parameter `nodename`. And so if the `nodename` for a cluster is `riakts-node-1`, you would need to generate your certificate with that in mind, as in this OpenSSL example: Bash

title: Sources Management
heading: Certificate-based Authentication#
text: Bash openssl req -new ... '/CN=riakts-node-1'

title: Sources Management
heading: Certificate-based Authentication#
text: Once certificates have been generated and configured on all the nodes in your Riak TS cluster, you need to perform a rolling restart. Once that process is complete, you can use the client certificate that you generated for the user `riakuser`. How to use Riak TS clients in conjunction with OpenSSL and other certificates varies from client library to client library.

title: Sources Management
heading: Certificate-based Authentication#
text: Once that process is complete, you can use the client certificate that you generated for the user `riakuser`. How to use Riak TS clients in conjunction with OpenSSL and other certificates varies from client library to client library. We strongly recommend checking the documentation of your client library for further information.

title: Sources Management
heading: PAM-based Authentication#
text: This section assumes you have set up a pluggable authentication module (PAM) service bearing the name `riak_pam`, either by creating a `pam.d/riak_pam` service definition specifying `auth` or other PAM services set up to authenticate a user named `riakuser`. As in the certificate-based authentication example above, the user’s name must be the same in both your authentication module and in Riak TS Security. If we want the user `riakuser` to use this PAM service on `localhost`, we need to add a `pam` security source in Riak and specify the name of the service:

title: Sources Management
heading: PAM-based Authentication#
text: As in the certificate-based authentication example above, the user’s name must be the same in both your authentication module and in Riak TS Security. If we want the user `riakuser` to use this PAM service on `localhost`, we need to add a `pam` security source in Riak and specify the name of the service: Bash

title: Sources Management
heading: PAM-based Authentication#
text: Bash riak-admin security add-source all 127.0.0.1/32 pam service=riak_pam

title: Sources Management
heading: PAM-based Authentication#

The following command would remove the source for `riakuser` on `localhost`, regardless of which source is being used:

title: Sources Management

title: Sources Management
heading: Delete Source#
text: Note on Removing Sources If you apply a security source both to `all` and to specific users and then wish to remove that source, you will need to do so in separate steps. The `riak-admin security del-source all ...` command by itself is not sufficient. For example, if you have assigned the source `password` to both `all` and to the user `riakuser` on the network `127.0.0.1/32`, the following two-step process would be required to fully remove the source: Bash riak-admin security del-source all 127.0.0.1/32 password riak-admin security del-source riakuser 127.0.0.1/32 password

title: Sources Management
heading: Client vs. Server Cipher Order#
text: By default, Riak TS prefers the cipher order setting, `honor_cipher_order`, to be set to `on`. If you prefer, however, that clients’ preferred cipher order dictate which cipher is chosen, set `honor_cipher_order` to `off`.

heading: Certificate Configuration#
text: If you are using any of the available security sources, including trust-based authentication, you will need to do so over a secure SSL connection. In order to establish a secure connection, ensure that each Riak TS node’s configuration files point to the proper paths for your generated certs. By default, Riak TS assumes that all certs are stored in each node’s `/etc` directory.

title: Sources Management
heading: Certificate Configuration#
text: In order to establish a secure connection, ensure that each Riak TS node’s configuration files point to the proper paths for your generated certs. By default, Riak TS assumes that all certs are stored in each node’s `/etc` directory. If you are using the newer, `riak.conf`-based configuration system, you can change the location of the `/etc` directory by modifying the `platform_etc_dir`:

title: Sources Management
heading: Referer Checks and Certificate Revocation Lists#
text: In order to provide safeguards against cross-site-scripting (XSS) and request-forgery attacks, Riak TS performs secure referer checks by default. Those checks make it impossible to serve data directly from Riak TS. To disable those checks, set the `secure_referer_check` parameter to `off`.

title: Sources Management
heading: Referer Checks and Certificate Revocation Lists#
text: Those checks make it impossible to serve data directly from Riak TS. To disable those checks, set the `secure_referer_check` parameter to `off`. If you are using certificate-based authentication, Riak TS will check the certificate revocation list (CRL) of connecting clients’ certificate by default.

title: Sources Management
heading: Referer Checks and Certificate Revocation Lists#
text: To disable those checks, set the `secure_referer_check` parameter to `off`. If you are using certificate-based authentication, Riak TS will check the certificate revocation list (CRL) of connecting clients’ certificate by default. To disable this behavior, set the `check_crl` parameter to `off`.

title: Sources Management
heading: How Sources Are Applied#
text: When managing security sources—any of the sources explained above—you always have the option of applying a source to either a single user, multiple users, or all users (`all`). If specific users and `all` have no sources in common, this presents no difficulty. But what happens if one source is applied to `all` and a different source is applied to a specific user?

title: Sources Management
heading: How Sources Are Applied#
text: If specific users and `all` have no sources in common, this presents no difficulty. But what happens if one source is applied to `all` and a different source is applied to a specific user? The more-specifically assigned source (i.e. the source applied to the user) will be considered a user’s security source.

title: Sources Management
heading: How Sources Are Applied#
text: But what happens if one source is applied to `all` and a different source is applied to a specific user? The more-specifically assigned source (i.e. the source applied to the user) will be considered a user’s security source. We’ll illustrate that with the following example, in which the `certificate` source is assigned to `all`, but the `password` source is assigned to `riakuser`:

title: Sources Management
heading: How Sources Are Applied#
text: The more-specifically assigned source (i.e. the source applied to the user) will be considered a user’s security source. We’ll illustrate that with the following example, in which the `certificate` source is assigned to `all`, but the `password` source is assigned to `riakuser`: Bash

title: Sources Management
heading: How Sources Are Applied#
text: Bash riak-admin security add-source all 127.0.0.1/32 certificate riak-admin security add-source riakuser 127.0.0.1/32 password

title: Sources Management
heading: How Sources Are Applied#
text: If we run `riak-admin security print-sources`, we’ll get the following output: Text

title: Sources Management
heading: How Sources Are Applied#
text: As we can see, `password` is set as the security source for `riakuser`, whereas everyone else will authenticate using `certificate`.

title: User Management
text: Riak TS security lets you to control authorization by creating, modifying, and deleting user characteristics and granting users selective access to Riak TS functionality. Users can be assigned one or more of the following characteristics:

title: User Management
text: Users can be assigned one or more of the following characteristics: `username` `groups` `password`

title: User Management
text: You may also assign users characteristics beyond those listed above, such as listing email addresses or other information, but those values will carry no special significance for Riak TS. Note The `username` cannot be changed once a user has been created.

title: User Management
heading: Add Group#
text: For easier management of permissions across several users, it is possible to create groups to be assigned to those users. Bash

title: User Management
heading: Add Group#
text: Bash riak-admin security add-group admin

title: User Management
heading: Add User#
text: To create a user with the username `riakuser`, we use the `add-user` command: Bash

title: User Management
heading: Add User#
text: Bash riak-admin security add-user riakuser

title: User Management
heading: Add User#
text: Using the command this way creates the user `riakuser` without any characteristics beyond a username, which is the only attribute that you must assign upon user creation. You may also assign a password or other attributes to the user upon creation. Here, we’ll assign a password:

title: User Management
heading: Add User#
text: You may also assign a password or other attributes to the user upon creation. Here, we’ll assign a password: Bash

title: User Management
heading: Add User#
text: Bash riak-admin security add-user riakuser password=Test1234

title: User Management
heading: Assigning a Password and Altering Existing User Characteristics#
text: While passwords and other characteristics can be set upon user creation, it often makes sense to change user characteristics after the user has already been created. Let’s say that the user `riakuser` was created without a password (or created with a password that we’d like to change). The `alter-user` command can be used to modify our `riakuser` user:

title: User Management
heading: Assigning a Password and Altering Existing User Characteristics#
text: Let’s say that the user `riakuser` was created without a password (or created with a password that we’d like to change). The `alter-user` command can be used to modify our `riakuser` user: Bash

title: User Management
heading: Assigning a Password and Altering Existing User Characteristics#
text: Bash riak-admin security alter-user riakuser password=opensesame

title: User Management
heading: Assigning a Password and Altering Existing User Characteristics#
text: When creating or altering a user, any number of `<option>=<value>` pairs can be appended to the end of the command. Any non-standard options will be stored and displayed via the `riak-admin security print-users` command. Bash

title: User Management
heading: Assigning a Password and Altering Existing User Characteristics#
text: Bash riak-admin security alter-user riakuser name=bill age=47 fav_color=red

title: User Management
heading: Assigning a Password and Altering Existing User Characteristics#
text: Now, the `print-users` command should return this: Text

title: User Management
heading: Assigning a Password and Altering Existing User Characteristics#

title: User Management
heading: Assigning a Password and Altering Existing User Characteristics#

title: User Management
heading: Assigning a Password and Altering Existing User Characteristics#
text: Note Usernames CANNOT be changed using the `alter-user` command. If you attempt to do so by running `alter-user riakuser username=other-name`, for example, this will add the `{"username","other-name"}` tuple to `riakuser`’s options.

title: User Management
heading: Managing Groups for a User#
text: If we have a user `jane_goodall` and we’d like to assign her to the `admin` group, we assign the value `admin` to the option `groups`: Bash

title: User Management
heading: Managing Groups for a User#
text: Bash riak-admin security alter-user jane_goodall groups=admin

title: User Management
heading: Managing Groups for a User#
text: If we’d like to make the user `jane_goodall` both an `admin` and an `archoverlord`: Bash

title: User Management
heading: Managing Groups for a User#
text: Bash riak-admin alter-user jane_goodall groups=admin,archoverlord

title: User Management
heading: Managing Groups for a User#
text: There is no way to incrementally add groups; even if `jane_goodall` was already an `admin`, it is necessary to list it again when adding the `archoverlord` group. Thus, to remove a group from a user, use `alter-user` and list all other groups. If the user should be removed from all groups, use `groups=` with no list:

title: User Management
heading: Managing Groups for a User#
text: Thus, to remove a group from a user, use `alter-user` and list all other groups. If the user should be removed from all groups, use `groups=` with no list: Bash

title: User Management
heading: Managing Groups for a User#
text: Bash riak-admin alter-user jane_goodall groups=

title: User Management
heading: Managing Groups for Groups#
text: Groups can be added to other groups for cascading permissions. Bash

title: User Management
heading: Managing Groups for Groups#
text: Bash riak-admin alter-group admin groups=dev

title: User Management
heading: Deleting a User or Group#
text: If you’d like to remove a user, use the `del-user` command: Bash

title: User Management
heading: Deleting a User or Group#
text: Bash riak-admin security del-user riakuser

title: User Management
heading: Deleting a User or Group#
text: For groups, use the `del-group` command: Bash

title: User Management
heading: Deleting a User or Group#
text: Bash riak-admin security del-group admin

title: User Management
heading: Adding or Deleting Multiple Users#
text: The `riak-admin security` command does not currently allow you to add or delete multiple users using a single command. Instead, they must be added or deleted one by one.

title: User Management
heading: Managing Permissions#
text: Permission to perform a wide variety of operations against Riak TS can be granted to, or revoked from, users via the `grant` and `revoke` commands.

title: User Management
heading: `grant`#
text: The `grant` command takes one of the following forms: Bash

title: User Management
heading: `grant`#
text: Bash riak-admin security grant <permissions> on any to all|{<user>|<group>[,...]} riak-admin security grant <permissions> on <table> to all|{<user>|<group>[,...]}

title: User Management
heading: `revoke`#
text: The `revoke` command is essentially the same, except that `to` is replaced with `from` of `to`: Bash

title: User Management
heading: `revoke`#
text: Bash riak-admin security revoke <permissions> on any from all|{<user>|<group>[,...]} riak-admin security revoke <permissions> on <table> from all|{<user>|<group>[,...]}

title: User Management
heading: Selecting `any` and `all`#
text: If you select `any`, the permission (or set of permissions) is granted/revoked for all tables. If you specify a table only, then the permission is granted/revoked for all tables of that type. Selecting `all` grants or revokes a permission (or set of permissions) for all users in all groups.

title: User Management
heading: Selecting `any` and `all`#
text: If you specify a table only, then the permission is granted/revoked for all tables of that type. Selecting `all` grants or revokes a permission (or set of permissions) for all users in all groups. When specifying the user(s)/group(s) to apply a permission (or set of permissions), you may list any number of users or groups comma-separated with no whitespace.

title: User Management
heading: Selecting `any` and `all`#
text: Selecting `all` grants or revokes a permission (or set of permissions) for all users in all groups. When specifying the user(s)/group(s) to apply a permission (or set of permissions), you may list any number of users or groups comma-separated with no whitespace. Here is an example of granting multiple permissions across all tables to multiple users:

title: User Management
heading: Selecting `any` and `all`#
text: When specifying the user(s)/group(s) to apply a permission (or set of permissions), you may list any number of users or groups comma-separated with no whitespace. Here is an example of granting multiple permissions across all tables to multiple users: Bash

title: User Management
heading: Selecting `any` and `all`#
text: Bash riak-admin security grant riak_ts.get on any to jane,ahmed

title: User Management
heading: Selecting `any` and `all`#
text: If the same name is used for both a user and a group, the `grant` command will ask for the name to be prefixed with `user/` or `group/` to disambiguate.

Access to this functionality should be granted very carefully. For example, if you’d like to create a `client` account that is allowed only to run `GET` and `PUT` requests on all tables:

title: User Management
heading: Riak TS Permissions#
text: Access to this functionality should be granted very carefully. For example, if you’d like to create a `client` account that is allowed only to run `GET` and `PUT` requests on all tables: Bash

title: User Management
heading: Riak TS Permissions#
text: Bash riak-admin security add-user client riak-admin security grant riak_ts.get,riak_ts.put on any to client

title: Time Representations in Riak TS
text: Timestamps are stored in Riak TS as epoch milliseconds, but TS also supports ISO 8601 string representations. This document will present the basics, but we highly recommend reading Learn About Timestamps for all the details. This is a time series database, after all.

title: Time Representations in Riak TS
text: This document will present the basics, but we highly recommend reading Learn About Timestamps for all the details. This is a time series database, after all. A Note on ISO 8601 Support ISO 8601 support is useful for casual interactions via riak shell, but we do NOT recommend using ISO 8601 in production applications.

title: Time Representations in Riak TS
text: This is a time series database, after all. A Note on ISO 8601 Support ISO 8601 support is useful for casual interactions via riak shell, but we do NOT recommend using ISO 8601 in production applications. Instead, use the TS-supported client libraries to pass timestamps as integers for better performance and correctness.

title: Time Representations in Riak TS
heading: ISO 8601 Guidelines#
text: Date/time strings in ISO 8601 are relatively straightforward to read and write. Some examples, all of which represent the same timestamp (`1470060351425000`):

title: Time Representations in Riak TS
heading: ISO 8601 Guidelines#
text: When using ISO 8601 strings for INSERT or SELECT statements, be sure to use single quotes around the string.

title: Time Representations in Riak TS
heading: Reduced Accuracy#
text: Strings that do not include seconds are referred to by the standard as reduced accuracy representations. A couple examples:

title: Time Representations in Riak TS
heading: Reduced Accuracy#
text: Using reduced accuracy for values in an `INSERT` will result in a millisecond UTC time that corresponds to the start of the time period in question. `2016-08` will map to midnight on August 1st 2016, for example. See Learn About Timestamps for the implications of using reduced accuracy in queries.

title: Time Representations in Riak TS
heading: Fractional Times#
text: Fractional times are particularly relevant given the millisecond accuracy in Riak TS timestamps. The string `2016-08-01 14:05:51.425Z` would be converted to the Riak TS millisecond timestamp `1470060351425`.

title: Time Representations in Riak TS
heading: Time Zones#
text: It is possible to define a cluster-wide default time zone, expressed as an offset from GMT. Its impact is limited to interpreting strings used for `SELECT` or `INSERT` that do not include a time zone specification. Text

title: Time Representations in Riak TS
heading: Time Zones#
text: Text $ riak-admin timezone not configured $ riak-admin timezone "-05:00" Success, timezone is now configured to '-05:00' $ riak-admin timezone -05:00

title: Time Representations in Riak TS
heading: Time Zones#
text: It is only necessary to do this on one of your cluster members. In the absence of such a configuration, the default time zone will be GMT.

title: Time Representations in Riak TS
heading: IMPORTANT: Daylight Saving Time#
text: There is a caveat when setting the default time zone. Defining a default time zone as a GMT offset means that when Daylight Saving Time begins or ends, the default time zone must be reconfigured for times to be translated correctly. You can schedule a cron job to adjust the time zone, but be aware that different implementations of cron handle DST transitions differently.

title: Time Representations in Riak TS
heading: IMPORTANT: Daylight Saving Time#
text: Defining a default time zone as a GMT offset means that when Daylight Saving Time begins or ends, the default time zone must be reconfigured for times to be translated correctly. You can schedule a cron job to adjust the time zone, but be aware that different implementations of cron handle DST transitions differently. For more information on time zones, see Learn About Timestamps.

title: Writing Data to Riak TS
text: Now that you’ve planned and activated your Riak TS table, you are ready to write data to it.

title: Writing Data to Riak TS
heading: Writing Data#
text: Riak TS allows you to write multiple rows of data at a time. To demonstrate, we’ll use the example table from earlier: SQL

title: Writing Data to Riak TS
heading: Writing Data#
text: SQL CREATE TABLE GeoCheckin ( id SINT64 NOT NULL, region VARCHAR NOT NULL, state VARCHAR NOT NULL, time TIMESTAMP NOT NULL, weather VARCHAR NOT NULL, temperature DOUBLE, PRIMARY KEY ( (id, QUANTUM(time, 15, 'm')), id, time ) )

title: Writing Data to Riak TS
heading: Writing Data#
text: Note on validation Riak TS validates all rows on the server side before writing occurs, checking the number of row elements and types. If any of the rows fails validation then none of the rows will be written. An error message will be returned with the index numbers of the invalid rows in the batch, the first item in the batch being index one.

title: Writing Data to Riak TS
heading: Guidelines#
text: Batches should not be too large. Our testing revealed 100 rows per write as a sweet spot, but you should expect different results depending on your hardware and schema. Writes will assume that fields are in the same order as they’ve been declared in the table. Timestamps should be in Unix epoch/UTC milliseconds or ISO 8601 format.

title: Writing Data to Riak TS
heading: Tuning Batches#
text: Batches of data from a single write are packaged for delivery to each destination server as a performance optimization. For Enterprise customers using MDC, those batches are sent to the remote cluster via realtime sync. It is possible to specify an approximate largest-batch size for tuning purposes.

title: Writing Data to Riak TS
heading: Tuning Batches#
text: For Enterprise customers using MDC, those batches are sent to the remote cluster via realtime sync. It is possible to specify an approximate largest-batch size for tuning purposes. By default, batches have a soft cap size of 1MB of data, which we’ve found to be a reasonable size to avoid network congestion.

title: Writing Data to Riak TS
heading: ISO 8601#
text: You must include single quotes around the ISO 8601 value. You cannot use reduced accuracy time representations. In other words, you must specify your time down to the second (or use fractional times).
